docs.title: Setting up the course environment
docs.text:
What you need first

Your machine card, administrator rights on your laptop and a good internet connection. The downloads add up to a few gigabytes, most of it Docker. The ideas behind the options are in Environments and reproducibility.

For the rest of the course, everybody needs the same three things: a Unix shell (bash or zsh), a package manager to install tools, and Docker to run containers. You install all three today: first the shell and the package manager, which are all that the lab needs, and then Docker. Installing it now leaves time to fix any problem before you need it. There are several ways to get them, and the right one depends on your laptop's operating system: keep your machine card at hand.

This page describes the three possible setups, which we call tracks. Follow the one for your operating system, unless your instructor tells you individually to use another one.

Track What you get Who it suits A. Native your own OS's terminal and package manager, plus Docker macOS and Linux laptops B. Linux VM an Ubuntu or Debian virtual machine on your laptop, the one you set up in the introductory course, with Docker inside everybody on Windows; on macOS or Linux, anyone who prefers to keep the course separate from their own system C. Cloud a Linux machine in GitHub Codespaces, used from the browser or VS Code laptops where neither A nor B works: managed laptops without administrator rights, low-spec machines, tablets

Whichever track you follow, the commands in the rest of the course are the same: you always work in a Linux-style shell.

And WSL?

On Windows there is another way to get Linux, WSL (the Windows Subsystem for Linux). It is well integrated with Windows, but when something goes wrong, fixing it needs a good understanding of how Windows, Linux and the virtual machine underneath fit together. Use WSL only if you already know what you're doing; otherwise use the VM (track B). If you do use it, the instructions are in WSL (advanced).

docs.title: Track A: native
docs.text:
For macOS and Linux. On Windows, use track B.

macOSLinux

macOS is already a Unix system, and its Terminal runs zsh, so you only need a package manager and Docker.

Install Homebrew, the package manager for macOS. Paste the command from brew.sh into the Terminal:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

It asks for your password and installs Apple's command-line developer tools if you don't have them (that takes a few minutes). At the end it prints "Next steps": two commands that add Homebrew to your PATH. Run them. Then check:

brew --version

You already have the shell and the package manager: only Docker is left.

docs.title: Track B: a Linux VM
docs.text:
Use the Ubuntu or Debian virtual machine you set up in the introductory course. Start it, open its terminal and do everything in the course inside the VM: the shell, the package manager (apt), Docker, VS Code and your projects. Your laptop's own operating system only runs the VM.

  • Keep your projects in your home folder inside the VM (~, which is /home/<you>), not in a folder shared with your laptop. Shared folders are slower and handle permissions differently, which breaks some tools.
  • Give the VM enough resources: at least 2 CPUs, 4 GB of memory and 30 GB of disk. Docker images take space. You change this in the VM's settings while it is shut down.
  • Shut the VM down when you aren't working, to free your laptop's memory.

Ubuntu and Debian are both Debian-based: the same apt commands work on both, and wherever the course says "Ubuntu", it applies to Debian too. Desktop installations don't always include curl and git, which the course uses from the start, so install them now:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git

If you don't have a working VM, tell your instructor.

docs.title: Track C: GitHub Codespaces
docs.text:
A codespace is a Linux machine in GitHub's cloud, with VS Code in the browser and Docker ready to use. Nothing is installed on your laptop. A personal GitHub account includes a free monthly quota (enough for about 60 hours on the smallest machine), and the GitHub Student Developer Pack raises it.

  1. Sign in to GitHub. Your instructor gives you the link to the course's starter repository.
  2. In the repository, click Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main.
  3. After a minute, VS Code opens in the browser. The Terminal panel at the bottom is a bash shell on Ubuntu.

Stop your codespace when you finish

A codespace consumes your quota while it runs. It stops on its own after 30 minutes of inactivity, but it's better to stop it yourself: on github.com/codespaces, … → Stop codespace.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Install Docker once your shell works. Docker needs about 20 GB of free disk for the program and the images, and on a Mac a recent macOS: Docker Desktop supports the current version and the two previous ones.

Not enough space, or an older macOS?

Skip Docker today and tell your instructor, then free space or update macOS. Everything else today, the lab included, works without it.

macOSLinux and the VM (track B)Codespace (track C)

Install Docker Desktop. Download it from docker.com/products/docker-desktop. Choose Apple Silicon or Intel according to the architecture on your machine card. Open the .dmg, drag Docker to Applications and start it. Accept the terms. You can skip signing in.

Install Docker Engine with Docker's installation script, which works on Ubuntu and Debian, and let your user run Docker without sudo:

curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Log out and in again (or restart the VM) for the group change to take effect. On other distributions, follow the official instructions at docs.docker.com/engine/install.

Docker is already installed.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Whatever your track, open the course shell (the macOS Terminal, the terminal on Linux or inside your VM, or the codespace terminal) and run:

echo $SHELL
uname -sm
curl --version | head -n 1
docker run --rm hello-world
What you should see
  • /bin/zsh or /bin/bash.
  • Darwin arm64 (or Darwin x86_64) on a Mac. Linux x86_64 or Linux aarch64 everywhere else: in the VM, in WSL and in a codespace you are on Linux.
  • A line starting with curl 8. (any version is fine).
  • Docker downloads a tiny image and prints a message that starts with Hello from Docker! and explains what just happened.

If docker says permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket, your user isn't in the docker group yet: log out and in again (or restart the VM). If it says Cannot connect to the Docker daemon, Docker isn't running: start Docker Desktop on macOS, or run sudo systemctl start docker on Linux.

Once the first three commands work, you're ready for the lab. The Docker check can wait until after the lab if Docker is still downloading.

docs.title: WSL (advanced)
docs.text:
The course supports Windows through the VM (track B). Use WSL only if you are already comfortable with it and can solve its problems on your own: in class, we help with the VM first.

WSL instructions: only if you know what you're doing

WSL (the Windows Subsystem for Linux) gives you a real Ubuntu, with bash and apt, integrated with Windows. Docker Desktop uses it too.

What WSL is

WSL lets Linux programs run on Windows without dual booting and without managing a VM yourself. Its current version, WSL 2, runs a real Linux kernel, built by Microsoft, inside a small, lightweight virtual machine that Windows starts and stops for you in a second or two. On top of that kernel you install a distribution (we use Ubuntu), which brings the usual Linux userland: bash, apt and the standard tools.

Unlike a VM you create yourself, WSL is integrated with Windows. Ubuntu appears as a tab in Windows Terminal; the Windows disk is visible from Linux at /mnt/c; your Linux files are visible from the File Explorer under Linux; and Windows programs (such as VS Code) can work on Linux folders. Docker Desktop uses the same lightweight VM to run Linux containers, which is why it needs WSL.

The older WSL 1 had no Linux kernel: it translated Linux system calls into Windows ones. It was slower for files and couldn't run Docker. wsl --install installs WSL 2.

1. Install WSL with Ubuntu. Right-click Terminal (or PowerShell) and choose Run as administrator. Then run:

wsl --install

This enables the virtualization components, installs the Linux kernel and the Ubuntu distribution. Restart Windows when it finishes.

If WSL is already installed with another distribution (or only with docker-desktop), wsl --install doesn't add Ubuntu. Run wsl --install -d Ubuntu instead. wsl --list --verbose shows what you have.

2. Create your Linux user. After the restart, open Ubuntu from the Start menu (it also appears as a tab in Windows Terminal). The first time, it asks for a user name and password for Linux. They are independent of your Windows account; choose something you'll remember, because sudo will ask for this password. Then update the system:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Work inside Ubuntu, not in PowerShell

From now on, open the Ubuntu terminal for the course and keep your projects in your Linux home folder (~, which is /home/<you>), not in /mnt/c/.... Files on the Windows disk are much slower to access from Linux, and their permissions behave differently.

If wsl --install fails, the most common cause is virtualization being disabled in the firmware (see Memory, disk and virtualization). If you can't fix it, use the VM.

3. Install Docker Desktop on Windows. Download it from docker.com/products/docker-desktop (choose ARM64 if your machine card says ARM64) and install it with the default options, which use WSL 2. Start it, then in Settings → Resources → WSL integration turn on the integration with Ubuntu.

With WSL, "the course shell" is the Ubuntu terminal, and the rest of the course works as on Linux.

docs.title: Python projects with uv
docs.text:
Most people learn Python in a notebook: open it, pip install whatever is missing, run the cells. That is fine for exploring data, and it is exactly how you get Ana's "works on my machine" problem. Software that a team builds, tests and deploys needs more. It needs a known Python version, its own environment and a standard way to run it. This session sets that up with uv: a single, fast tool that manages Python versions, virtual environments and projects.

By the end, ledger is a Python project with its own Python and environment, ready for its code.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. Python projects and environments. What the interpreter is and what Python versions mean for compatibility. Where installed packages go, why every project needs its own virtual environment, and what pyproject.toml declares.
  2. Lab: the ledger becomes a Python project. You install uv and a specific Python, create the ledger project, run it in its own environment, and see requires-python refuse an older Python.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the session you should be able to:

  • Explain what the Python interpreter does, and what a project's requires-python protects against.
  • Explain what a virtual environment is, why each project needs its own, and how uv run uses it.
  • Read the [project] and [project.scripts] sections of a pyproject.toml.
  • Install a Python version with uv, create a project with uv init and run it with uv run.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the course environment and the ~/smd/ledger folder with the transactions file (see A ledger in the shell). If you don't have the folder, the start of the lab has the two commands that create it and download the data. Basic Python is assumed: variables, lists, dictionaries, loops and functions. If you need a refresher, the official Python tutorial (sections 3 to 5) covers it.

docs.title: Lab: the ledger becomes a Python project
docs.text:
What you need first

The course environment and the folder ~/smd/ledger with data/transactions.csv (see A ledger in the shell). The concepts are in Python projects and environments.

If you don't have the ledger folder

This lab only needs the data file. These commands create the folder and download the file:

mkdir -p ~/smd/ledger/data
cd ~/smd/ledger
curl -fsSL -o data/transactions.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ami232/ie-smd/main/data/transactions.csv

ls data should show transactions.csv.

In the shell, balance.sh answered one question with awk. In this lab you turn ~/smd/ledger into a Python project: a pinned Python version, its own virtual environment and a command called ledger, ready for its code.

Work in the course shell (the macOS Terminal, the terminal on Linux or inside your VM, or the codespace; the Ubuntu terminal if you use WSL).

docs.title: 1. Install uv
docs.text:
macOSLinux, VM, codespace, WSL 
brew install uv

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

The installer puts uv in ~/.local/bin and adds that folder to your PATH in your shell's startup file. Open a new terminal (or run source $HOME/.local/bin/env) so the shell sees it.

Then check:

uv --version
What you should see

A line such as uv 0.13.6. Any recent version works. If you get command not found, it is the PATH problem: open a new terminal.

If your prompt starts with (base): conda

If you installed Anaconda or Miniconda, your prompt may start with (base). This means conda's base environment is active in every terminal, so python3 and pip are conda's. In the next steps you compare the system Python with the project's Python, and with conda active the results are confusing. VS Code may also suggest conda's Python instead of the project's. Turn it off for this course:

conda deactivate
conda config --set auto_activate_base false

The first command turns it off in this terminal. The second stops it from turning on in new terminals (if conda says the setting is deprecated, use conda config --set auto_activate false). Conda stays installed, and conda activate base turns it on when you need it. Open a new terminal: the (base) should be gone.

docs.title: 2. Install a Python version
docs.text:
First, see what your system already has:

python3 --version
which python3

This is the system Python: the one your operating system uses for its own tools. It may be missing, or a different version on each machine (Ubuntu 24.04 comes with 3.12; macOS may have none, or the 3.9 from Apple's developer tools). Don't rely on it for projects. Ask uv for the exact version we use instead:

uv python install 3.14
uv python list --only-installed
What you should see

uv downloads a standalone build of Python 3.14 (about 30 MB) and reports something like Installed Python 3.14.10. The list shows it next to any Python your system already had. uv keeps its own Pythons in its own folder and never touches the system one.

docs.title: 3. Create the project
docs.text:
Go into the ledger folder and turn it into a project:

cd ~/smd/ledger
uv init --package --vcs none --python 3.14
  • --package creates an installable package with a command-line entry point (not just a script).
  • --vcs none skips creating a Git repository: the project goes into Git on its own, with a repository on GitHub.
  • --python 3.14 pins the project to Python 3.14.

Look at what it created, including hidden files:

ls -a
cat pyproject.toml
cat .python-version
cat src/ledger/__init__.py
What you should see

Your existing files (data/ and, if you made them, balance.sh and report.txt) are untouched. Next to them there are four new ones: .python-version (contains 3.14), README.md, pyproject.toml and src/ledger/__init__.py.

pyproject.toml is like the one explained in the concepts page: requires-python = ">=3.14", no dependencies yet, and a script ledger = "ledger:main". If your Git configuration has your name, uv adds an authors line too. The package contains a single function:

def main() -> None:
    print("Hello from ledger!")

docs.title: 4. First run
docs.text:
uv run ledger

The first time, uv creates the virtual environment and installs the project in it. Then it runs the ledger command, which calls main(). Now look at the environment:

ls -a
ls .venv/bin
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
What you should see 
Using CPython 3.14.10
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
...
Hello from ledger!

There are now a .venv folder and a uv.lock file. uv.lock lists the exact packages installed in .venv; for now only ledger itself, as the project has no dependencies yet. It becomes important when the project gets its first dependency. .venv/bin contains python and ledger, the command defined in [project.scripts]. The last command prints a path ending in ledger/.venv/bin/python3: uv run uses the project's own Python, not the system one.

docs.title: 5. requires-python at work
docs.text:
Try to pin the project to an older Python:

uv python pin 3.13
What you should see 
error: The requested Python version `3.13` is incompatible with the project `requires-python` value of `>=3.14`.

(uv may first download Python 3.13.) The project declares that it needs 3.14 or newer, and uv enforces it. This error, at setup time, is what would have saved Ana from the SyntaxError on the server (see It works on my machine).

docs.title: Python projects and environments
docs.text:
What you need first

The layers of an environment and the idea of reproducibility, from Environments and reproducibility. Environment variables and PATH, from Users, packages and the environment.

docs.title: From a script to a project
docs.text:
Ana's fraud script from It works on my machine was a script: one file, run by hand, depending on whatever happened to be installed on her laptop. Scripts are great for exploring. Once other people need to run the code, though, on other machines and for months, it becomes a project, and it needs four things the script didn't have:

  1. A declared Python version, so nobody runs it on an interpreter that can't understand it.
  2. Its own set of installed libraries, separate from those of every other project on the machine.
  3. A precise list of those libraries and their versions, so that every installation is identical.
  4. A standard way to run it, documented in the project itself.

This page explains the version, the environment and the way to run it, and the lab builds them with uv. The precise list of libraries comes with the project's first dependency (see Dependencies and the lockfile).

docs.title: The interpreter
docs.text:
When you run python3 report.py, the program python3 is the interpreter. It reads your source code, translates it into an intermediate form called bytecode and executes it, instruction by instruction. The standard interpreter, the one you download from python.org or that uv installs, is called CPython because it is written in C.

This is different from languages like C, Go or Rust, which are compiled: a compiler turns the source code into machine code for one processor and one operating system before it runs, and you distribute the result. Python code, by contrast, is distributed as source, and it runs wherever there is a suitable interpreter. That makes the interpreter itself part of the environment, with two consequences:

  • The interpreter must be installed on every machine that runs the code. A container image for a Python application always starts from an image that already has Python.
  • Its version matters, because each version understands a slightly different language.

docs.title: Python versions
docs.text:
Python versions have the form 3.14.2: major, minor and patch numbers. Python has been at major version 3 since 2008. A new minor version comes out every October, adding features to the language and to the standard library. Each one receives bug fixes and then security fixes for five years, after which it reaches its end of life. Patch versions (3.14.1, 3.14.2…) only fix bugs and never change the language.

Code is forward compatible within major version 3, with few exceptions: code written for 3.10 almost always runs on 3.14. The reverse is not true. Code that uses something new fails on older versions:

Feature Since What happens on an older Python match statement 3.10 SyntaxError before anything runs tomllib module (read TOML files) 3.11 ModuleNotFoundError type aliases (type Amount = Decimal) 3.12 SyntaxError

That is why a project declares the oldest Python it supports, with requires-python = ">=3.14" in its configuration. Tools refuse to install the project on anything older, so the error happens at installation with a clear message, not in production with a confusing one.

Which version should a new project use? Usually the newest one that all your libraries support. A brand-new Python version takes a few months to be supported by every library that includes compiled code, so professional teams often stay one version behind the newest during its first months. In this course we use Python 3.14.

docs.title: Imports and site-packages
docs.text:
When Python runs import pandas, it searches a list of folders, sys.path, for a module or package called pandas. One of those folders is the interpreter's site-packages, and that is where installing a package puts it. Installing is just downloading a package (usually a wheel, a ready-to-install .whl archive) from the Python Package Index (PyPI, pypi.org) and unpacking it into site-packages.

That works well for one project. Now imagine two projects on the same laptop. Project A was written two years ago with pandas 1.5. Project B is new and needs pandas 2.3. There is only one site-packages per interpreter, so there can be only one pandas. Install 2.3 for project B, and project A breaks. This is the classic dependency conflict, and the more projects you have, the worse it gets.

docs.title: Virtual environments
docs.text:
The solution is to give each project its own site-packages.

Definition: virtual environment

A virtual environment (venv) is a folder, conventionally called .venv inside the project, that contains a link to a Python interpreter and its own empty site-packages. Packages installed in it are visible only to programs that run with that environment's Python, .venv/bin/python.

Inside the venv there is a bin folder with its own python and the command-line programs of the installed packages. Running code "in the environment" just means using that python. There are two ways to do so:

  • Activate the environment: source .venv/bin/activate puts .venv/bin at the front of your PATH (that is all it does), so python now means the venv's Python. deactivate undoes it.
  • Let a tool choose it: uv run report.py finds the project's .venv, creates or updates it if needed, and runs the command with its Python. You never activate anything, so you can't forget to.

A virtual environment is disposable. It is built from the project's files, it is not committed to Git, and if it gets into a strange state you delete it and rebuild it. It is also specific to one machine: it contains absolute paths and, for compiled libraries, code for one operating system and architecture. You never copy a .venv to another computer; you rebuild it there.

docs.title: pyproject.toml
docs.text:
Every modern Python project is described by one file, pyproject.toml, written in the TOML format (sections in [brackets], then key = value lines). This is the one uv init creates in the lab:

[project]
name = "ledger"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = []

[project.scripts]
ledger = "ledger:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.6,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
  • [project] holds the standard metadata: the name, the version of your project, the supported Python and the list of direct dependencies. It is empty for now, because ledger has no dependencies yet.
  • [project.scripts] creates a command: ledger will run the function main of the package ledger. This is the "standard way to run it" from the start of the page.
  • [build-system] says which tool turns the project into an installable package. You won't need to touch it.

The structure is a standard (it is the same for every tool), so the project doesn't depend on uv: pip and others can read it too.

docs.title: uv
docs.text:
For years, Python developers needed several tools for all this: pyenv to install Python versions, venv or virtualenv for environments, pip to install packages, pip-tools or Poetry for lockfiles, pipx for command-line tools. uv does all of it in one program, and much faster (it is written in Rust). These are the commands for creating and running a project:

Command Does uv python install 3.14 downloads and installs a Python version, independently of the system's uv python list shows the Python versions uv can find, its own and the system's uv init --package creates a project: pyproject.toml, .python-version, src/<name>/ uv run <cmd> runs a command in the project's environment, creating the environment first if needed uv python pin 3.14 changes the project's Python version in .python-version

The file .python-version (just 3.14) tells uv which Python to use for the project's environment, and uv downloads it if it's missing. The commands for adding libraries to a project are in uv commands for dependencies.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using pip install on the system Python. It mixes the packages of every project, and on recent Linux and macOS versions it is refused with an externally-managed-environment error, precisely to prevent this. Install libraries in a project's environment instead.
  • Committing .venv. It is large, specific to one machine and rebuilt in seconds. Commit the files that describe the project (pyproject.toml, .python-version, src/) and ignore .venv.
  • "It works in my notebook." A notebook's kernel may use a completely different Python and packages than your project. If the code is part of the project, run it with uv run.

Key takeaways

  • Python code runs on an interpreter, which is part of the environment. New language features fail on older versions, so a project declares requires-python.
  • Installed packages go into the interpreter's site-packages. A virtual environment gives each project its own, avoiding conflicts. It is disposable and is rebuilt, never copied.
  • pyproject.toml describes the project: its name, the Python it needs (requires-python) and the commands it provides ([project.scripts]).
  • uv installs Python versions, creates projects and runs commands in the project's environment with uv run.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A colleague's code starts with import tomllib and fails with ModuleNotFoundError on the server, though it works on their laptop. What is the likely cause, and what line in pyproject.toml would have caught it earlier?

Solution

tomllib was added to the standard library in Python 3.11, so the server is running an older Python. If the project declared requires-python = ">=3.11" (or higher), installing it on the server would have failed at once with a clear message about the Python version, instead of failing when the code ran.

2. Explain what source .venv/bin/activate changes, and why uv run ledger works without it.

Solution

Activating only puts .venv/bin at the front of the PATH variable of the current shell, so commands like python or ledger are found in the virtual environment first. uv run doesn't need that, because it finds the project's environment itself (from the pyproject.toml of the current folder or its parents), creates or updates it if needed, and runs the command with it directly.

docs.title: Lab: writing and checking the ledger
docs.text:
What you need first

The ledger project (see The ledger becomes a Python project): the folder ~/smd/ledger with pyproject.toml, src/ledger/__init__.py and .venv, where uv run ledger prints Hello from ledger!. The concepts of dependencies are in Dependencies and the lockfile.

You add a third-party library, which gives the project a lockfile, and prove that the project rebuilds from its files (steps 4 to 6). docs.title: 1. Set up VS Code
docs.text: From here on you write Python. A plain text editor saves the file, but it doesn't help you write it. Set up VS Code, the editor we use for the rest of the course, and connect it to the project.

docs.title: Install VS Code and the code command
docs.text:
You open projects from the terminal with the code command, so VS Code must be installed and code must be in your PATH.

macOSLinux and the VMWindows with WSL (advanced) 
brew install --cask visual-studio-code

Homebrew installs the app in Applications and puts code in its own folder of the PATH. If Homebrew says the app already exists, you installed VS Code earlier from a download: keep it, and skip to the check below.

On Linux, and on Windows inside the VM, VS Code runs inside Linux, next to your files. In a web browser (inside the VM if you use one), download the .deb package from code.visualstudio.com/download: x64 if uname -m prints x86_64, Arm64 if it prints aarch64. Then install it from the terminal:

sudo apt install ~/Downloads/code_*.deb

The package puts code in your PATH and adds Microsoft's repository, so sudo apt upgrade keeps VS Code up to date.

Only if you use WSL instead of the VM (see WSL (advanced)). VS Code runs on Windows, not inside Ubuntu. In PowerShell:

winget install -e --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode

or download the installer from code.visualstudio.com and keep the option Add to PATH checked. Then open VS Code, go to the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for WSL and install the extension by Microsoft. Close VS Code.

With the WSL extension, the VS Code window runs on Windows, and a small server runs inside Ubuntu. The files, Python and uv stay in Linux, where the rest of the course runs.

Now open a new terminal (inside the VM if you use one) and check:

code --version
What you should see

Three lines: a version number such as 1.106.0, a long commit identifier and the architecture (arm64 or x64).

If you get command not found, the code command is not in your PATH:

  • macOS, VS Code installed from a download: move Visual Studio Code to the Applications folder if it isn't there, and open it. Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P), type shell command and choose Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH. Open a new terminal and try again.
  • Linux and the VM: the package didn't install. Check the output of sudo apt install for an error.
  • WSL: close every Ubuntu terminal and open a new one. WSL adds the folders of the Windows PATH to Linux's PATH when the terminal starts, so a terminal opened before installing VS Code doesn't see code.

docs.title: Open the project
docs.text:
cd ~/smd/ledger
code .

. is the current folder: you are telling VS Code to open the folder you are in. VS Code calls an open folder a workspace.

What you should see

A VS Code window with the project's files in the Explorer on the left: .venv, data, src, .python-version, pyproject.toml, README.md and uv.lock.

  • macOS: VS Code asks Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder? Choose Yes, I trust the authors: they are your own files.
  • WSL: the first time, VS Code installs its server in Ubuntu, which takes a few seconds. The bottom-left corner shows WSL: Ubuntu. If it doesn't, the window is working on Windows files: close it and run code . again from the Ubuntu terminal. Don't open the folder from the Windows File Explorer.

Open the Extensions view (Cmd+Shift+X on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+X on Linux, in the VM and on Windows), search for Python and install the extension Python by Microsoft. With WSL, the button says Install in WSL: Ubuntu: extensions that work with your code run on the Linux side, next to it.

Pylance needs to know which Python runs the project, to know which libraries are installed and where. VS Code usually marks it as Recommended.

Then open a terminal inside VS Code with Terminal → New Terminal (Ctrl+`):

pwd

What you should see

The status bar at the bottom right shows the Python version (3.14) and .venv. The terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already in the project folder: pwd prints .../smd/ledger, and uv run ledger prints Hello from ledger!.

With WSL, this terminal is bash in Ubuntu, the same shell as the Ubuntu terminal.

docs.title: 2. Write the ledger
docs.text:
In VS Code, open src/ledger/__init__.py from the Explorer on the left, and run the commands of this lab in VS Code's terminal. If you can't use VS Code, any text editor works: nano src/ledger/__init__.py in the terminal (Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits) or TextEdit on macOS in plain-text mode.

Replace the contents of the file with the following, and save it (Cmd+S on macOS, Ctrl+S on Linux, in the VM and on Windows). A dot on the file's tab means it has unsaved changes, and uv run only sees what is saved:

"""ledger: balances and spending from a CSV file of transactions."""

import argparse
import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal


def read_transactions(path):
    """Reads the CSV file and returns one dict per row, with the amount as a Decimal."""
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        transactions = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    for t in transactions:
        t["amount"] = Decimal(t["amount"])
    return transactions


def totals_by(transactions, column):
    """Adds up the amounts for each value of `column` (account, category...)."""
    totals = defaultdict(Decimal)
    for t in transactions:
        totals[t[column]] += t["amount"]
    return dict(totals)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="ledger", description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("command", choices=["balance", "spending"])
    parser.add_argument("file", nargs="?", default="data/transactions.csv")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    transactions = read_transactions(args.file)
    if args.command == "balance":
        for account, total in sorted(totals_by(transactions, "account").items()):
            print(f"{account:<10} {total:>10}")
    else:
        spending = [t for t in transactions if t["amount"] < 0 and t["category"] != "transfer"]
        for category, total in sorted(totals_by(spending, "category").items(), key=lambda item: item[1]):
            print(f"{category:<14} {total:>10}")

Type it rather than pasting it, and notice what the editor does: it completes names (Decim + Tab gives Decimal), shows the documentation of a function when you hover over it, and underlines in red anything it doesn't understand.

What it does:

  • read_transactions uses the standard csv module. DictReader turns each row into a dictionary keyed by the header (t["account"], t["amount"]…). Each amount becomes a Decimal from its string. Step 3 explains why.
  • totals_by adds up the amounts grouped by any column. This is the same idea as s[$2] += $5 in balance.sh.
  • main uses the standard argparse module to read the command line: a command (balance or spending) and an optional file, which defaults to data/transactions.csv.

Run it:

uv run ledger balance
uv run ledger spending
uv run ledger --help
uv run ledger total
What you should see 
checking      3349.10
savings        906.00

The same balances as balance.sh in the shell. Then the spending by category, most negative first:

housing          -2850.00
groceries         -797.60
restaurants       -320.09
transport         -135.57
health            -119.70
subscriptions      -77.94

--help prints a usage message that argparse generated for free. ledger total fails with invalid choice: 'total' (choose from 'balance', 'spending'), and echo $? would print 2: a proper error and a proper exit code, unlike the shell script.

docs.title: 3. Money is not a float
docs.text:
ledger handles money, and the code above stores every amount as a Decimal, not a float. Here is why. Python's float stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions, like 0.1, have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. The error is tiny, but it shows up:

print(0.1 + 0.2)

0.30000000000000004

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

False

Adding up many amounts accumulates these errors. These are the payments to a gym in three months, as floats:

print(-39.90 + -39.90 + -39.90)

-119.69999999999999

The standard library's Decimal type stores numbers in decimal, exactly as written, so sums of amounts with two decimals are exact. Create a Decimal from a string, not from a float, or you copy the float's error into it:

from decimal import Decimal

print(Decimal("-39.90") + Decimal("-39.90") + Decimal("-39.90"))

-119.70

print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))

True

print(Decimal(0.1))  # created from a float: the binary error is now visible

0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

In a report, a balance of 3349.0999999999995 looks careless. In a payment system, an amount that is one cent wrong is a reconciliation problem, and comparisons such as balance == 0 can fail when they shouldn't. The rule in financial software is simple: money is never a float. In Python you use Decimal. In databases you use a NUMERIC column, or store amounts as integers in cents, as ledger does when it moves to a database.

Now see it in ledger: break it on purpose. In read_transactions, change Decimal(t["amount"]) to float(t["amount"]). In totals_by, change defaultdict(Decimal) to defaultdict(float). Run both commands again:

uv run ledger balance
uv run ledger spending
What you should see 
checking   3349.0999999999995
savings         906.0

and, among the categories, health -119.69999999999999. Same data, same logic, and wrong-looking money. Undo both changes before you continue, and check that uv run ledger balance prints 3349.10 again.

Question. A teammate stores amounts as floats and writes if balance == 0: close_account(). After a deposit of 0.10, a deposit of 0.20 and a withdrawal of 0.30, the account is not closed. Explain why, and show the fix.

Solution

With floats, 0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3 is 5.551115123125783e-17, not 0, because 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are not exactly representable in binary. The comparison is false and the account stays open with a "balance" of a few hundred-quadrillionths of a euro. With decimals created from strings, Decimal("0.10") + Decimal("0.20") - Decimal("0.30") is exactly Decimal("0.00"), which equals 0, so the comparison works.

docs.title: 4. Add a dependency
docs.text:
Plain columns of text are fine, but a table is easier to read. The rich library draws tables in the terminal. Add it to the project:

uv add rich

Now look at what changed:

grep -A2 "^dependencies" pyproject.toml
uv tree
grep -c "^\[\[package\]\]" uv.lock
What you should see

pyproject.toml now lists one direct dependency with a constraint, such as "rich>=15.0.0". uv tree shows rich and its three transitive dependencies (markdown-it-py, mdurl, pygments). uv.lock has 5 packages: those four plus ledger itself, each with an exact version and file hashes. Your versions may be newer than the ones shown in Dependencies and the lockfile.

Use rich in the spending command. At the top of __init__.py, after from decimal import Decimal, add:

from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

In VS Code, these two lines must not be underlined: if they are, the selected interpreter is not the project's (step 1). Then replace the last two lines of main (the for loop of spending) with:

        table = Table(title="Spending by category")
        table.add_column("Category")
        table.add_column("EUR", justify="right")

            table.add_row(category, f"{-total:,.2f}")
        Console().print(table)

docs.title: 5. Isolation
docs.text:
rich is installed in the project's environment, and only there. Check it from outside the project's environment:

python3 -c "import rich"
uv run python -c "import rich; print('rich is here')"
What you should see

The system Python fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rich' (or python3: command not found if your system has none). Through uv run, the import works. Your other projects, and your system, are unaffected by what you install in ledger.

docs.title: 6. Rebuild from the files
docs.text:
The environment is disposable. Delete it and rebuild it:

rm -rf .venv
uv sync
uv run ledger balance

Now simulate a teammate who receives the project. Copy only the files that define it to a new folder, and run it there:

mkdir -p /tmp/ledger-copy
cp -r pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version README.md src data /tmp/ledger-copy/
cd /tmp/ledger-copy
uv run ledger spending
cd ~/smd/ledger
What you should see

After rm -rf .venv, uv sync recreates it and installs the same five packages in well under a second. The packages are in uv's cache, so nothing is downloaded again. In the copy, uv run creates a new environment from the lockfile and prints the same table.

These files are what goes into a Git repository. .venv is not among them.

docs.title: 7. Debug the ledger
docs.text: When a program gives a wrong result, the first reflex is to add print calls, run it again, read the output and remove the print calls. A debugger does the same job without changing the code: it stops the program at the lines you choose, shows every variable at that moment, and lets you run the rest one line at a time.

docs.title: Tell VS Code how to run ledger
docs.text:
VS Code's default debug configuration runs the file open in the editor, without arguments. ledger is a command that needs an argument (spending), so you describe how to run it in a file called .vscode/launch.json.

In the Explorer, click the New File icon next to the project's name, type .vscode/launch.json and press Enter. VS Code creates the folder and the file. Paste this and save:

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ledger spending",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/ledger",
            "args": ["spending"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal"
        }
    ]
}
  • "name" is the name you choose from a list when you start debugging.
  • "type": "debugpy" uses the Python Debugger extension.
  • "program" is the ledger command that uv created in .venv/bin when you first ran the project (see First run). ${workspaceFolder} is the project folder. This is what uv run ledger runs: the command imports the ledger package and calls main().
  • "args" are the command-line arguments, the same words you type after uv run ledger.
  • "console": "integratedTerminal" shows the program's output in VS Code's terminal.

docs.title: Stop at a breakpoint
docs.text:
Open src/ledger/__init__.py and find the line inside totals_by that adds up the amounts:

        totals[t[column]] += t["amount"]

Click just to the left of its line number. A red dot appears: that is a breakpoint, a line where the debugger stops before running it.

Open the Run and Debug view (Cmd+Shift+D on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+D on Linux, in the VM and on Windows), check that ledger spending is selected at the top, and click the green triangle (or press F5).

What you should see

The program starts and stops at the breakpoint: the line is highlighted in yellow and a toolbar with the debugging buttons appears at the top. On the left:

  • Variables → Locals shows the variables of totals_by at this moment: column is 'category', totals is an empty defaultdict, transactions is a list of 44 transactions (the 56 transactions minus income, interest and transfers), and t is the first of them, the rent:

    {'date': '2026-01-01', 'account': 'checking', 'description': 'Rent', 'category': 'housing', 'amount': Decimal('-950.00')}

  • Call Stack shows how the program got here: main called totals_by. Click main to see its variables (args, transactions, spending), then click totals_by again.

docs.title: Step through the code
docs.text:
The debugging toolbar has six buttons. From left to right, with their keys:

Button Key What it does Continue F5 run until the next breakpoint Step Over F10 run the current line and stop at the next one Step Into F11 go inside the function called on the current line Step Out Shift+F11 finish the current function and stop where it was called Restart Shift+Cmd+F5 / Ctrl+Shift+F5 start again Stop Shift+F5 end the program

On a Mac laptop, the function keys may need Fn, and F11 may show the desktop: use the buttons instead.

Press Step Over twice and watch the Variables panel. The loop runs the highlighted line, goes back to for t in transactions, and stops on the highlighted line again with the next transaction. Values that just changed are highlighted.

Now use the Debug Console, the tab next to the terminal at the bottom. It evaluates any Python expression in the program's current state. Type, one at a time:

t["description"]
dict(totals)
len(transactions)
sum(t["amount"] for t in transactions)
What you should see

After two steps, t is the second transaction (Carrefour, -65.15) and totals contains {'housing': Decimal('-950.00')}. In the Debug Console: 'Carrefour', the same dictionary, 44, and Decimal('-4300.90'), the total spending of the three months.

docs.title: A conditional breakpoint
docs.text:
Stepping through 44 transactions one by one is slow. A conditional breakpoint stops only when an expression is true. Right-click the red dot, choose Edit Breakpoint…, type this expression and press Enter:

t["category"] == "health"

Press Continue. The program runs until the first health transaction. Use Step Over and Continue to follow totals["health"] through the three gym payments.

What you should see

The program stops at the gym membership of 10 January (-39.90). totals has no health key yet. After Step Over it has Decimal('-39.90'). At the next two stops (10 February and 10 March), the total goes to -79.80 and then, after the last step, -119.70.

This is the line where the float version of step 3 produced -119.69999999999999. With Decimal, the sum is exact.

Remove the breakpoint (click the red dot) and press Continue. The program runs to the end, and the table appears in the terminal.

Exercise. Add a second configuration to launch.json that runs ledger balance, and use it to stop in totals_by while it adds up the accounts. What is the value of column this time?

Solution

configurations is a list: add a second object, separated from the first by a comma. Then choose ledger balance from the list at the top of the Run and Debug view.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ledger spending",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/ledger",
            "args": ["spending"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal"
        },
        {
            "name": "ledger balance",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/ledger",
            "args": ["balance"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal"
        }
    ]
}

column is 'account', and transactions has all 56 transactions, because balance doesn't filter them.

docs.title: 8. Lint and format with Ruff
docs.text:
Ruff does two jobs. As a linter, it reads the code without running it and reports problems: names that are not defined, imports that are not used, and many patterns that usually hide a bug. As a formatter, it rewrites the layout of the code (spaces, line breaks, quotes) in one standard style, so that a whole team writes code that looks the same and a code review shows only real changes.

Ruff is a tool for whoever develops the project, not something ledger needs to run. Add it as a development dependency:

uv add --dev ruff
grep -A3 "dependency-groups" pyproject.toml
What you should see 
[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "ruff>=0.17.4",
]

Your version may be newer. Development dependencies go in their own group, separate from dependencies. uv.lock pins Ruff too, so the whole team uses the same version and gets the same results.

docs.title: The linter
docs.text:
Run it on the project:

uv run ruff check

It prints All checks passed!. Now introduce a typo. In totals_by, change for t in transactions: to for t in transaction: and save. Before running anything, look at the editor: Pylance underlines transaction and, when you hover over it, says "transaction" is not defined. Run Ruff, then the program:

uv run ruff check
uv run ledger spending
What you should see

Ruff finds the problem and shows where it is (your line numbers may be different):

F821 Undefined name `transaction`
  --> src/ledger/__init__.py:24:14
   |
22 |     """Adds up the amounts for each value of `column` (account, category...)."""
23 |     totals = defaultdict(Decimal)
24 |     for t in transaction:
   |              ^^^^^^^^^^^
25 |         totals[t[column]] += t["amount"]
26 |     return dict(totals)
   |

Found 1 error.

The program fails with NameError: name 'transaction' is not defined. Did you mean: 'transactions'?. Python only finds the error when it reaches that line. Ruff found it without running anything, and in a big program that line might only run in a case nobody tested.

Fix the typo and check that uv run ruff check prints All checks passed! again.

docs.title: The formatter
docs.text:
Ask Ruff what it would change, without changing anything yet:

uv run ruff format --diff
What you should see

A diff: lines starting with - would be removed, and lines starting with + would be added. Ruff wants to split the two lines of main that are longer than 88 characters:

-        spending = [t for t in transactions if t["amount"] < 0 and t["category"] != "transfer"]
+        spending = [
+            t for t in transactions if t["amount"] < 0 and t["category"] != "transfer"
+        ]

and the same for the for category, total in sorted(...) line.

Now apply it, and check that the program still does the same:

uv run ruff format
uv run ledger spending
What you should see

Ruff reports 1 file reformatted. VS Code shows the new layout of __init__.py, and ledger spending prints the same table as before: a formatter changes how the code looks, never what it does. Run uv run ruff format again: there is nothing left to change.

Ruff has hundreds of rules, and a project chooses which ones to apply in pyproject.toml. For now the defaults are enough. If you want to see Ruff's messages as you type, install the Ruff extension (by Astral) from the Extensions view.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
You have finished the lab when:

  • code . opens ~/smd/ledger in VS Code (with WSL, the bottom-left corner shows WSL: Ubuntu), with .venv as the interpreter;
  • uv run ledger balance prints 3349.10 and 906.00, and uv run ledger spending prints the table;
  • ~/smd/ledger contains uv.lock, and you can explain which files a teammate needs, and why .venv is not one of them;
  • .vscode/launch.json runs ledger spending under the debugger, and you can stop it in totals_by and read t and totals;
  • ruff is a development dependency in pyproject.toml, and uv run ruff check and uv run ruff format --diff report nothing to fix.

Challenge (optional). Add a third command, ledger months, that prints the net change (income minus spending, transfers included) for each month: 2026-01, 2026-02, 2026-03. Hint: t["date"][:7] gives the month of a transaction. You could add it as a key to each transaction and reuse totals_by.

Result to check

The three months sum to the net total of both accounts, 4255.10:

2026-01    1375.22
2026-02    1440.07
2026-03    1439.81

docs.title: Dependencies and the lockfile
docs.text:
What you need first

Virtual environments, pyproject.toml and the basic uv commands, from Python projects and environments, and the ledger project (see The ledger becomes a Python project).

A project needs four things: a declared Python version, its own environment, a standard way to run it, and a precise list of the libraries it uses. The first three are explained in From a script to a project. So far ledger only uses Python's standard library, so the list is empty. The moment it needs a library from PyPI, the project needs that fourth thing, and this page explains how it works.

docs.title: Direct and transitive
docs.text:
The libraries your code imports are its direct dependencies. They have dependencies of their own, which you also need: these are transitive dependencies. In the lab, ledger depends on one library, rich, which draws tables in the terminal. But installing it brings four packages:

ledger v0.1.0
└── rich v15.0.0
    ├── markdown-it-py v4.2.0
    │   └── mdurl v0.1.2
    └── pygments v2.21.0

A typical web application has a dozen direct dependencies and a hundred transitive ones. Any of them can change.

docs.title: Version constraints
docs.text:
You declare a direct dependency with a constraint, a range of acceptable versions, such as rich>=15.0.0. Constraints rely on a convention called semantic versioning: in MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, a new major version may break your code, a minor one adds features without breaking anything, and a patch only fixes bugs. Many projects follow it, some loosely.

Constraint Means rich any version rich>=15.0 15.0 or newer, including a future 16.0 that may break things rich>=15.0,<16 any 15.x: features and fixes, no breaking changes rich==15.0.0 exactly that version

Constraints alone are not enough for reproducibility. rich>=15.0 installs today's newest version today and a different one next month, and the same goes for every transitive dependency. Two people installing the "same" project a month apart can get different code.

docs.title: The lockfile
docs.text:
Definition: lockfile

A lockfile records the exact version of every package the project needs, direct and transitive, with a hash of each file to verify the download. It is generated by a tool from the constraints, committed to the repository, and used to install exactly the same packages everywhere.

The two files have different jobs. pyproject.toml says what the project accepts (its constraints). It is written by people. uv.lock says what the project uses (the resolved versions). It is written by the tool. Changing a dependency means editing the constraints, usually with uv add or uv remove, and letting the tool update the lock. When you want newer versions, you upgrade deliberately (uv lock --upgrade), run the tests, and commit the new lockfile, so the change is visible and reviewable.

docs.title: uv commands for dependencies
docs.text:
Command Does uv add rich adds a dependency: updates pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .venv uv add --dev ruff adds a dependency only for development (tests, linters), in its own group uv remove rich removes a dependency uv sync makes .venv match uv.lock exactly (installs, upgrades, removes) uv tree shows the dependency tree uv lock --upgrade resolves again with the newest versions the constraints allow

uv run also syncs the environment before running, so after a teammate changes the lockfile, your next uv run installs what changed. Together, .python-version, pyproject.toml and uv.lock describe layers 4 and 5 of the environment completely. Anyone who has uv can rebuild them identically, which is exactly the "automate it" level of reproducibility from session 1.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Not committing uv.lock. Without it, the project is not reproducible: every installation resolves the constraints again.
  • Editing the lockfile by hand. It is generated. Change the constraints, with uv add or uv remove, and let uv update it.
  • Constraints that are too loose or too tight. With rich alone, any future version is accepted, even one that breaks the code. With rich==15.0.0, the project never gets bug fixes, and it can't be installed next to another library that needs a newer rich. A lower bound such as rich>=15.0.0, which is what uv add writes, plus the lockfile, is the usual choice.

Key takeaways

  • Direct dependencies are the ones your code imports; they bring their own transitive dependencies.
  • pyproject.toml declares the direct dependencies with constraints, a range of acceptable versions. It is written by people.
  • The lockfile, uv.lock, pins every package to an exact version, with hashes. It is written by uv. Commit both files.
  • uv add and uv remove change the constraints and the lockfile together; uv sync makes .venv match the lockfile.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. In the dependency tree above, which dependencies are direct and which transitive? If rich stopped needing pygments in a future version, what would you have to change in pyproject.toml?

Solution

rich is the only direct dependency of ledger. markdown-it-py, mdurl and pygments are transitive: ledger gets them because rich needs them. You wouldn't change anything in pyproject.toml, because pygments is not listed there. After upgrading rich (uv lock --upgrade-package rich), uv would drop pygments from uv.lock, and uv sync would uninstall it from .venv.

2. Your pyproject.toml says pandas>=2.0. Today, uv locks pandas 2.3.3. Six months later a teammate clones the repository. (a) With the lockfile committed, which version does uv sync install for them? (b) And if the lockfile was not committed?

Solution
  • (a) Exactly 2.3.3, the version in uv.lock, whatever is newer on PyPI. That is the point of the lockfile.
  • (b) uv resolves the constraint again, so they get the newest version that satisfies >=2.0 six months later, maybe 2.4 or even a 3.0 that breaks the code. The two of you would be running different code without knowing it.

docs.title: Version control and collaboration with Git
docs.text: Until now, ledger lived only in a folder on your laptop, and its only history was your memory. In this session it gets a real history and a home on GitHub. You learn how Git records a project as a series of snapshots, how a local repository and GitHub exchange work, and how a team works in parallel with branches, combines that work with merges, deals with conflicts and reviews changes through pull requests. Then you do all of it, by hand, in the repository where you will build your application for the rest of the course.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. Version control with Git. Commits, the working tree and the staging area, .gitignore, remotes, branches, merges, conflicts, pull requests, tags, and how a team works on one repository.
  2. Lab: your app's repository. You create your repository on GitHub, add the ledger, and go through the whole workflow: commit, push, pull, branch, conflict and pull request. You submit the URL of your repository on Blackboard. This lab is done without AI.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the session you should be able to:

  • Explain what a commit is, and move changes from the working tree to the staging area and into a commit.
  • Decide which files of a project go into the repository, and keep the rest out with .gitignore.
  • Create a repository on GitHub, clone it, and exchange commits with it using push and pull.
  • Create a branch, commit on it and publish it.
  • Explain when a merge is a fast-forward and when it needs a merge commit.
  • Resolve a merge conflict by editing the file, and finish the merge.
  • Open a pull request with a useful description and merge it with a merge commit.
  • Mark a commit with a tag, push the tag, and link to that commit on GitHub.
  • Compare Gitflow and trunk-based development, and apply the workflow of a team that shares one repository: a protected main, one short-lived branch per task and small pull requests.

docs.title: Lab: your app's repository
docs.text:
What you need first

The ledger project in ~/smd/ledger (see Writing and checking the ledger), a GitHub account (see Create your GitHub account), and the concepts of Version control with Git. If your ledger isn't finished, you can start from the reference version, as explained in step 4.

Do this lab by hand, without AI

In this lab, AI assistants are not allowed: type every command yourself and read what Git answers. Don't ask a chatbot for the commands, and turn off inline suggestions in VS Code for today (if you use Copilot: click the Copilot icon in the status bar and disable completions).

Git is the safety net for everything else you do in this course, including the code you will write with AI: when an assistant breaks your project, Git is how you get it back. You can only trust a safety net you understand. Once you know what each command does, you can use AI for Git as for the rest of the course, under the rules in Using AI.

In this lab you create the repository where you will build your application for the rest of the course, and you go through the whole Git workflow once, on purpose: commits, pushing and pulling, a change made on GitHub, a branch, a conflict and a pull request. The repository's history is the proof that you did each step, so do them in order and don't rewrite it afterwards.

Submission. At the end, you submit the URL of your repository on Blackboard. The checkpoint lists what is checked.

docs.title: 1. Check Git and sign in to GitHub
docs.text:
Work in the course shell (the macOS Terminal, the terminal on Linux or inside your VM; the Ubuntu terminal if you use WSL). Check that Git is installed:

git --version

If you get command not found: on macOS, run xcode-select --install; on Linux and in the VM, sudo apt install -y git.

Install the GitHub CLI, gh, and sign in. It configures Git to use your GitHub login, so you never type a password or manage keys:

macOSLinux, VM, WSL 
brew install gh

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y gh

gh auth login

Answer the questions with the arrow keys and Enter: GitHub.com, HTTPS, Yes (authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials), Login with a web browser. gh prints a one-time code; press Enter, paste the code in the browser page that opens, and authorize. Then check:

gh auth status
What you should see

Logged in to github.com account <your-username>, with Git operations protocol: https. If the browser doesn't open (some VMs), open github.com/login/device yourself and type the code.

docs.title: 2. Configure Git
docs.text:
Git records an author in every commit. Tell it your name and email, once per computer:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "ID+username@users.noreply.github.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase false
git config --global core.editor nano
  • For the email, use your GitHub no-reply address: on GitHub, Settings → Emails, under "Keep my email addresses private". It looks like 12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com. Your commits will be public, and this keeps your real address out of them. It also links the commits to your GitHub account.
  • pull.rebase false tells git pull to combine histories with a merge. Without it, recent versions of Git refuse a pull when both sides have new commits, which you will do in step 9.
  • core.editor nano makes Git open nano if it ever needs you to write a message. In nano, Ctrl+O and Enter save, Ctrl+X exits.
git config --global --list
What you should see

Your five settings, among others: user.name=..., user.email=...@users.noreply.github.com, init.defaultbranch=main, pull.rebase=false and core.editor=nano.

docs.title: 3. Create the repository on GitHub and clone it
docs.text:
On github.com, click + → New repository (top right) and fill in:

  • Repository name: smd-app.
  • Public. Your repository is public: it is part of your portfolio, and it is how your work is checked.
  • Add README: on.
  • Add .gitignore: choose the Python template.
  • No license for now.

Click Create repository. GitHub makes the first commit for you, with the two files. Now copy the repository to your laptop. On the repository's page, click Code, choose HTTPS and copy the URL. Then:

cd ~/smd
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/smd-app.git
cd smd-app
ls -a
git log
git status
What you should see

git clone prints Cloning into 'smd-app'... and creates the folder. ls -a shows .git (the history), .gitignore and README.md. git log shows one commit, "Initial commit", by you, with its full hash. git status says On branch main, Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main' and nothing to commit, working tree clean.

docs.title: 4. Add the ledger and commit
docs.text:
Copy the files that describe and build the ledger project into the repository. These are the files a teammate needs (see Rebuild from the files); .venv is not one of them:

cp -r ~/smd/ledger/{pyproject.toml,uv.lock,.python-version,src,data} .
uv run ledger balance
My ledger is not finished

Use the reference version. On github.com/ami232/ie-smd-ledger, switch to the tag ledger-script (button main → Tags), click Code → Download ZIP, unzip it, and copy the same five items from the unzipped folder instead of from ~/smd/ledger. Don't copy its README.md or .gitignore: your repository has its own.

uv run creates .venv inside the repository. Look at what Git sees:

git status
What you should see

Under Untracked files: .python-version, data/, pyproject.toml, src/ and uv.lock. There is no .venv: the Python .gitignore from GitHub lists it, so Git ignores it. ledger balance printed 3349.10 and 906.00, as before.

Stage the files, check exactly what will be recorded, and commit:

git add .
git status
git diff --staged --stat
git commit -m "Add the ledger project"
git log --oneline
What you should see

After git add ., the five items are under Changes to be committed. git diff --staged --stat lists the files and how many lines each adds. The commit prints its short hash and 5 files changed or similar. git log --oneline shows two commits, newest first.

Now a second commit, for the README. Open the repository in VS Code (code .) and replace the contents of README.md with this, keeping the exact second line, which you will need in step 9:

# smd-app

Personal finance ledger: balances and spending from a CSV file.

## Run it

    uv run ledger balance
    uv run ledger spending

Save it and commit it from the terminal:

git status
git diff
git add README.md
git commit -m "Describe the app and how to run it"
What you should see

git diff shows the old README lines with - and the new ones with +. After the commit, git status says Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits: you have two commits that GitHub doesn't have yet.

docs.title: 5. Push
docs.text:
git push
git status
What you should see

git push prints a few lines ending in main -> main. git status says Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'. Refresh the repository's page on GitHub: the files are there, the README shows its new text, and the commit count says 3 commits.

docs.title: 6. Change something on GitHub
docs.text:
Changes can also come from GitHub: a teammate's work, or an edit in the browser. Make one. On the repository's page, open README.md, click the pencil icon (Edit this file), and add at the end:

## Author

<your-github-username>

Click Commit changes…, keep "Commit directly to the main branch", write a message such as Add author and confirm. Your laptop doesn't have this commit yet.

docs.title: 7. Pull
docs.text:
git status
git pull
git log --oneline
cat README.md
What you should see

The first git status still says up to date with 'origin/main': Git only knows about the remote what it saw at the last push or pull. git pull downloads the new commit and reports Fast-forward, since only GitHub had new work. git log shows four commits, the newest being yours from the browser, and the README now ends with the Author section.

docs.title: 8. Create a branch, commit and push it
docs.text:
Work on a new feature in its own branch. Create it and move to it:

git switch -c feature/roadmap
git branch

In README.md, make two changes:

  1. Change the second line (the description) to:

    Personal finance ledger: balances, spending and monthly reports from a CSV file.

  2. Add this section before Author:

    ## Roadmap

- Monthly report of income and spending
- A database instead of a CSV file
- A web API and a dashboard

Save, commit and publish the branch:

git add README.md
git commit -m "Add a roadmap"
git push -u origin feature/roadmap
What you should see

git branch lists main and * feature/roadmap (the * is where you are). The push creates the branch on GitHub: the output includes * [new branch] feature/roadmap -> feature/roadmap and a link to create a pull request (not yet). On GitHub, the branch selector (the main button) now lists feature/roadmap.

docs.title: 9. Create a conflict and resolve it
docs.text:
While you were working on the branch, someone changed main. Do it yourself: on GitHub, make sure the branch selector says main, open README.md, click the pencil, and change the same second line to:

Personal finance ledger for the command line.

Commit it directly to main. Now main and your branch have both changed the same line. Bring main's new work into your branch:

git pull origin main
What you should see 
Auto-merging README.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

Git combined everything it could and stopped at the line both sides changed. git status says You have unmerged paths and lists README.md under Unmerged paths.

Open README.md. The second line is now:

<<<<<<< HEAD
Personal finance ledger: balances, spending and monthly reports from a CSV file.
=======
Personal finance ledger for the command line.
>>>>>>> 1a2b3c4d5e6f...

HEAD is your branch's version; the other one comes from main on GitHub (the long code is its commit hash). Resolve it by editing the text yourself: replace the five lines, markers included, with one description that keeps both ideas:

Personal finance ledger for the command line: balances, spending and monthly reports from a CSV file.

Check that no marker is left, then finish the merge:

grep -n "<<<<<<<\|=======\|>>>>>>>" README.md
git add README.md
git commit --no-edit
git log --oneline --graph
git push
What you should see

grep prints nothing: no markers left. git commit --no-edit creates the merge commit with Git's default message, Merge branch 'main' of https://github.com/.... In git log --oneline --graph, two lines of history join at that commit: your roadmap commit on one side, the browser edit on the other. git push sends the merge to your branch on GitHub.

docs.title: 10. Open and merge a pull request
docs.text:
On GitHub, open the Pull requests tab and click New pull request. Choose base: main and compare: feature/roadmap. GitHub shows the differences and Able to merge, because you already resolved the conflict on the branch. Click Create pull request and fill in:

  • Title: Add a roadmap
  • Description: two or three sentences: what the branch changes, and how you resolved the conflict in the description line.

Click Create pull request. Read the Files changed tab, as a reviewer would. Then, in the Conversation tab, merge it: check that the green button says Merge pull request (if it says Squash and merge or Rebase and merge, use the arrow next to it to choose Create a merge commit), click it and confirm. GitHub offers to delete the branch: you can.

Finally, bring the result to your laptop and tidy up:

git switch main
git pull
git branch -d feature/roadmap
git log --oneline --graph --all
What you should see

git pull fast-forwards main to the merge commit GitHub created (Merge pull request #1 from <your-username>/feature/roadmap). git branch -d deletes the local branch, which is safe because its commits are now in main. The graph shows the whole lab: the initial commit, your two commits, the browser edit, the branch with its roadmap commit, the merge that resolved the conflict, and the merge of the pull request. The README on GitHub has the combined description, the roadmap and the author.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Submit the URL of your repository (https://github.com/<your-username>/smd-app) on Blackboard. Don't change the history after submitting: no force pushes, and don't delete the repository. Your repository should show:

  • a public repository with pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version, src/ and data/, and no .venv;
  • commits made from your laptop, with your name and your no-reply email;
  • a commit made on GitHub's website;
  • a branch other than main, pushed to GitHub, with its own commit;
  • on that branch, a merge of main that resolved a conflict, with no markers left;
  • a pull request from that branch to main, with a description, merged with a merge commit.

This repository is where you build your application: from here on, every change to it goes through Git.
