docs.title: Version control with Git
docs.text:
What you need first

The shell from Linux and the shell: moving between folders, hidden files (ls -a) and running commands. The ledger project (see Writing and checking the ledger), and which of its files describe the project and which are generated, from Dependencies and the lockfile.

docs.title: Why version control
docs.text:
Your ledger folder has changed many times: a shell script, then a Python project, then real code, a dependency and a lockfile. If tomorrow uv run ledger spending stopped working, could you say what changed since it last worked? Could you go back to last week's version? Most people's first answer is to copy the folder: ledger_old, ledger_v2, ledger_final, ledger_final_REALLY. That works for a day. After a month nobody knows which copy is which, what changed between two of them, or why.

Now add a team. Four people edit the same project. Ana changes read_transactions while Ben adds a command to main. They email files to each other, and one of them overwrites the other's work without noticing. On a real team, with real money in the data, this is how bugs reach production and nobody can say when they arrived.

A version control system solves both problems. It records every saved state of the project with who saved it, when and why, it lets several people work on the same files at the same time, and it combines their work, warning when two changes collide. Git is the version control system almost everyone uses today, and GitHub is the most popular website for hosting Git projects and working on them as a team.

docs.title: Commits: snapshots of the project
docs.text:
Git records the history of a project as a sequence of commits. Think of a commit as a photograph of every file of the project at one moment, with a caption: the author, the date and a message saying what changed and why. You decide when to take the photograph, typically after each small piece of work that makes sense on its own ("add the spending command", "store amounts as Decimal").

Definition: repository and commit

A repository (repo) is a project folder whose history Git tracks. The history is stored in a hidden folder, .git, at the top of the project.

A commit is a snapshot of all the tracked files of the repository, together with its author, date, message and a reference to the previous commit (its parent). Each commit is identified by a hash, a 40-character code computed from its contents, such as 7259904e1c…, usually shortened to its first 7 characters.

Because each commit points to its parent, the commits form a chain: the history. git log shows it, newest first. Because the hash is computed from the contents, including the parent's hash, nobody can change an old commit without changing every hash after it. Git notices, which is what makes the history trustworthy.

Commits are cheap. Git stores only the files that changed between snapshots and compresses them, so committing often costs almost nothing.

docs.title: The three areas
docs.text:
Taking a snapshot is a two-step process, and this is the part of Git that confuses people most at first. Your files live in three places:

  1. The working tree: the files in the folder, as you edit them.
  2. The staging area (also called the index): the changes you have selected for the next commit.
  3. The repository: the commits already recorded in .git.

git add copies a change from the working tree to the staging area. git commit records everything in the staging area as a new commit. git status tells you, at any moment, what is changed but not staged, what is staged, and what Git doesn't track at all.

 working tree  ──git add──▶  staging area  ──git commit──▶  repository
  (your files)               (next commit)                 (history in .git)

Why two steps? Because you often change several things at once and want to record them as separate commits. If you fixed a bug in totals_by and also updated the README, git add src/ledger/__init__.py and a commit "fix totals for empty files", then git add README.md and a commit "document the spending command", gives a history where each commit has one purpose. When something breaks later, a history like that tells you which change caused it.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
You have just edited the README of a repository. These are the commands and what each one shows:

git status                   # README.md is listed as "modified", in red: changed, not staged
git diff                     # the changed lines: - for removed, + for added
git add README.md
git status                   # README.md is now under "Changes to be committed", in green
git commit -m "Describe what the app does"
git log --oneline            # the new commit is at the top, with its short hash

The message after -m is for people: write what the commit does and, if it isn't obvious, why. "Describe what the app does" helps someone reading the history in three months. "changes" or "asdf" doesn't.

docs.title: What goes in the repository
docs.text:
A repository should contain everything needed to rebuild the project, and nothing that can be rebuilt from it or that must stay private. For ledger:

Commit Don't commit pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version .venv/: generated by uv, specific to your machine src/, README.md __pycache__/, .ruff_cache/: generated by Python and Ruff sample data the code needs (data/transactions.csv) .env files with passwords or keys

A file called .gitignore, at the top of the repository, lists the patterns of files Git must ignore. A line .venv/ makes Git ignore the whole folder: git status doesn't show it, and git add . doesn't add it. GitHub offers ready-made .gitignore templates for each language when you create a repository.

Secrets in Git are forever

If you commit a password or an API key, deleting the file in the next commit doesn't remove it: it is still in the history, and anyone with a copy of the repository can find it. Public repositories on GitHub are scanned by bots looking for keys within minutes. If it happens, the only safe fix is to revoke the key and create a new one. Session 12 explains how to keep secrets out of the code.

docs.title: Local and remote repositories
docs.text:
So far, everything happens on your laptop: Git doesn't need a server. To share the project, and to keep a copy that survives a broken laptop, you connect your repository to a remote: a copy of the same repository on a server, usually GitHub.

Definition: remote, clone, push and pull

A remote is another copy of the repository that yours knows about, by a name and a URL. The default name is origin.

  • git clone <url> downloads a repository with its whole history and sets it up as origin.
  • git push sends your new commits to the remote.
  • git pull downloads the new commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch. It is two operations in one: git fetch (download) followed by git merge (combine).

Your local repository and the remote are independent copies: a commit you make on your laptop is not on GitHub until you push it, and a change someone makes on GitHub is not on your laptop until you pull it. git status tells you when your branch is "ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits" (you have commits to push) or "behind" (there are commits to pull).

GitHub needs to know who you are before it accepts a push. With the GitHub CLI (gh), gh auth login signs you in once through the browser and configures Git to use that login, so you don't type passwords or manage keys.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
On a team, several pieces of work are in progress at the same time: Ana's new command, Ben's bug fix, a teammate's experiment that may never be finished. If everyone committed to the same line of history, each person's half-finished work would break the project for the others. Branches let each piece of work have its own line of history until it is ready.

Definition: branch

A branch is a movable name that points to a commit. When you commit on a branch, the branch moves forward to the new commit. main is the branch that holds the project's official history. HEAD is the branch you are on now.

A branch costs almost nothing: it is a name and a 40-character hash. The usual workflow is to create a branch for each piece of work, commit on it, and bring it back into main when it's done and reviewed:

git switch -c feature/monthly-report   # create the branch and move to it
# ...edit, add, commit, as many times as needed...
git push -u origin feature/monthly-report   # publish the branch on GitHub
git switch main                          # go back to main
git branch                               # list the local branches; * marks the current one

-u (short for --set-upstream) links the local branch to the one on GitHub, so that from then on a plain git push or git pull on this branch knows where to go. Branch names are free text; prefixes like feature/ and fix/ are a common convention that makes them easier to read.

docs.title: Merging and conflicts
docs.text:
When the work on a branch is finished, you merge it: you bring its commits into another branch, usually main. There are two cases.

If main has not moved since the branch was created, Git just moves main forward to the branch's last commit. This is a fast-forward: no new commit is needed. It is also what usually happens when you git pull and only the remote has new commits.

If both branches have new commits, Git creates a merge commit, a commit with two parents that combines both lines of work. Git combines the changes on its own, line by line, as long as they touch different parts of the files. Two people editing different functions of the same file is fine.

Before the merge, main and feature/monthly-report have both moved on since commit B:

gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature/monthly-report
    commit id: "D"
    commit id: "E"
    checkout main
    commit id: "C"
git switch main
git merge feature/monthly-report

After the merge, main has a new commit M with two parents, C and E:

%%{init: {'gitGraph': {'showCommitLabel': true, 'rotateCommitLabel': false}, 'themeVariables': {'git0': '#78909c', 'gitBranchLabel0': '#ffffff', 'git1': '#26a69a', 'gitBranchLabel1': '#ffffff', 'git2': '#ffb74d', 'gitBranchLabel2': '#000000', 'git3': '#9575cd', 'gitBranchLabel3': '#ffffff', 'git4': '#4fc3f7', 'gitBranchLabel4': '#000000', 'git5': '#e57373', 'gitBranchLabel5': '#ffffff', 'commitLabelFontSize': '13px', 'tagLabelFontSize': '12px'}}}%%
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature/monthly-report
    commit id: "D"
    commit id: "E"
    checkout main
    commit id: "C"
    merge feature/monthly-report id: "M"

A conflict happens when both branches changed the same lines of the same file. Git can't know which version is right, so it stops the merge and asks you. It writes both versions into the file, between markers:

<<<<<<< HEAD
Personal finance ledger: balances, spending and monthly reports.
=======
Personal finance ledger for the command line.
>>>>>>> main

The part between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your version (the branch you are on). The part between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming version. To resolve the conflict, you edit the file so it contains what it should contain (one version, the other, or a combination), delete the three marker lines, then git add the file and git commit to finish the merge. VS Code highlights the conflicts and offers buttons (Accept Current, Accept Incoming, Accept Both), but the decision is always yours: Git can't know what the text means.

A conflict is not an error. It is Git refusing to guess. The usual cause is two people working on the same part of the code at the same time, and the best prevention is small branches that are merged often.

docs.title: Pull requests and code review
docs.text:
On GitHub, a branch doesn't usually go into main with a plain git merge. Instead, you open a pull request (PR): a proposal to merge a branch, with a title and a description of what it changes and why. GitHub shows the differences, and teammates review them: they read the code, comment on specific lines, ask for changes or approve. When the PR is approved, someone clicks Merge, and GitHub makes the merge on the server.

Code review is how teams keep quality up and spread knowledge: at least two people have read every change before it reaches main, and both of them understand it. In the group project, every change to main goes through a reviewed pull request.

GitHub offers three ways to merge a PR. Create a merge commit keeps every commit of the branch and adds a merge commit, so the history shows exactly what happened. Squash and merge combines all the commits of the branch into one. Rebase and merge copies the commits onto main without a merge commit. In this course we use merge commits, because the history is part of what we assess.

docs.title: Tags: a name for one commit
docs.text:
A branch is a name that moves: each new commit on main takes the name main with it. Sometimes you need the opposite, a name that stays on one commit forever: the version 1.0 that you released, or the exact state of your repository that you hand in. That is a tag.

Definition: tag

A tag is a name attached to one commit, which doesn't move when new commits are added. It is used to mark versions (v1.0, v1.1…) and any state of the project that other people need to find again exactly.

git tag cp2                       # tag the current commit (HEAD) as cp2
git tag -a v1.0 -m "First release"   # an annotated tag: with an author, a date and a message
git tag                           # list the tags
git log --oneline --decorate -3   # the tags appear next to their commits: (HEAD -> main, tag: cp2)
git push origin cp2               # send the tag to GitHub

A tag without options is a lightweight tag: just the name. An annotated tag (-a) also records who created it, when and why, and is the usual choice for released versions. Both point to one commit in the same way.

git push doesn't send tags: you push each one by name, as in the last line. Until you do, the tag exists only on your computer. On GitHub, the repository's Tags page (https://github.com/<user>/<repo>/tags) lists them, each with the id of its commit. Clicking the id opens the page of that commit, whose address, https://github.com/<user>/<repo>/commit/<hash>, is a permanent link to that exact state of the project.

A tag is meant not to move. If you tagged the wrong commit, you can move it with -f (force), and you must force the push too, because you are replacing a tag that GitHub already has:

git tag -f cp2                    # move cp2 to the current commit
git push -f origin cp2            # replace the tag on GitHub
git tag -d cp2                    # or delete it locally...
git push origin --delete cp2      # ...and on GitHub

Move or delete only your own tags, and only before anyone relies on them: a team that has deployed v1.0 must be able to trust that v1.0 is always the same code.

In this course, you mark the commit you hand in for each checkpoint with a tag (cp2, cp3…), and you submit the link to that commit on Blackboard. What is graded is that commit, whatever you push afterwards.

docs.title: Working as a team on one repository
docs.text:
Branches, merges and pull requests are the mechanics. A team also needs to agree on how to use them: which branches exist, how long they live, and how work gets into main. Without an agreement, six people working on one repository step on each other: someone pushes half-finished code to main and breaks it for everybody, a branch lives for two weeks and conflicts with everything when it is finally merged, and nobody knows which version works.

Definition: branching strategy

A branching strategy (or Git workflow) is a team's agreement on which branches exist, what each one is for, how long it lives, and how changes move from one to another.

Two strategies dominate in practice.

docs.title: Gitflow
docs.text:
Gitflow uses several long-lived branches:

  • main contains only released versions, each one tagged (v1.0, v1.1…);
  • develop is where finished features are integrated;
  • feature/* branches start from develop and go back to it;
  • release/* branches prepare a release: they start from develop and are merged into main and back into develop;
  • hotfix/* branches fix a released version: they start from main and are merged into main and develop.

Gitflow fits software that is released in versions on a schedule, sometimes with several versions in use at once: a mobile app that goes through store review, a product installed on customers' servers, a library. It is heavy for anything else: every feature goes through two merges, and develop and main drift apart.

docs.title: Trunk-based development
docs.text:
In trunk-based development, there is one long-lived branch, main (the trunk), and it must always work. Every change is a short-lived branch that lives hours or a day or two, goes through a pull request with review and automated checks, and is merged into main. The version of it that most teams on GitHub use is called GitHub flow.

%%{init: {'gitGraph': {'showCommitLabel': false}, 'themeVariables': {'git0': '#78909c', 'gitBranchLabel0': '#ffffff', 'git1': '#26a69a', 'gitBranchLabel1': '#ffffff', 'git2': '#ffb74d', 'gitBranchLabel2': '#000000', 'git3': '#9575cd', 'gitBranchLabel3': '#ffffff', 'git4': '#4fc3f7', 'gitBranchLabel4': '#000000', 'git5': '#e57373', 'gitBranchLabel5': '#ffffff', 'commitLabelFontSize': '13px', 'tagLabelFontSize': '12px'}}}%%
gitGraph
    commit
    branch feature/invoices-api
    commit
    checkout main
    branch fix/dashboard-totals
    commit
    checkout main
    merge fix/dashboard-totals
    checkout feature/invoices-api
    commit
    checkout main
    branch feature/login
    commit
    checkout feature/invoices-api
    merge main
    commit
    checkout main

    checkout feature/login
    commit
    merge main
    checkout main
    merge feature/login
    commit

Three tasks overlap here, as they do in a real team: fix/dashboard-totals is opened and merged while feature/invoices-api is still in progress, and feature/login starts before feature/invoices-api is merged. Before their pull requests are merged, the two longer branches bring main into themselves (git pull origin main), so they are tested with everybody else's work.

Trunk-based development fits web applications that are deployed continuously: every merge into main can go to production, because continuous integration checks every pull request. It requires discipline: changes must be small, and nobody may break main.

Gitflow Trunk-based (GitHub flow) Long-lived branches main, develop main only Feature branches can live for weeks hours or a few days Releases release/* branches, on a schedule any merge into main can be deployed Conflicts large, at the end small, every day Fits versioned releases, large teams, several versions in use web applications, continuous deployment, small teams

docs.title: The workflow for a small team
docs.text:
For a team of six or seven building one web application in a few weeks, trunk-based development is the better choice. The application is deployed from main, there is only one version in use, and the main risk is integrating late, which is exactly what short-lived branches prevent. Gitflow would add a develop branch, release branches and double merges, and solve problems the team doesn't have.

In practice, a team agrees on five rules:

  1. Nobody pushes to main. Protect it on GitHub: Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule (or Settings → Rulesets) for main, requiring a pull request with at least one approval and, once there is continuous integration, the checks to pass. GitHub then refuses a direct git push to main, for everybody.
  2. One branch per task, created from an up-to-date main, and named after the task: feature/invoices-api, fix/dashboard-totals, docs/readme-conventions.
  3. Small pull requests, merged within a day or two. A pull request that changes a few files is reviewed in minutes; one that changes half the project waits for days and conflicts with everybody's work.
  4. Bring main into your branch often, and resolve conflicts on your branch, before the pull request is merged. The button Update branch on the pull request does the same on GitHub when there is no conflict.
  5. Split the code so that people rarely edit the same files: one package, API router and page per module. Files that everybody needs (the application setup, the configuration, the CI workflow) have an owner, and changes to them go through that person.

Each task follows the same loop:

git switch main
git pull                                  # start from the latest main
git switch -c feature/invoices-api        # one branch for this task
# ...edit, git add, git commit, as many times as needed...
git pull origin main                      # bring in what others merged meanwhile
git push -u origin feature/invoices-api   # publish the branch
# open a pull request on GitHub, linked to its issue ("Closes #12")
# a teammate reviews it; when it is approved and the checks pass, merge it
git switch main
git pull                                  # main now has your work
git branch -d feature/invoices-api        # the branch is done

Writing Closes #12 in the description of a pull request links it to issue 12, and GitHub closes the issue when the pull request is merged, so the project board stays up to date on its own. If you want early feedback on unfinished work, open the pull request as a draft: teammates can read and comment on it, but it can't be merged until you mark it as ready.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Committing without checking git status first. You commit files you didn't mean to (.venv, a .env with a password) or forget the ones you did. Run git status before every commit, and git diff --staged to see exactly what you're about to record.
  • Working on main for everything. It works alone, but on a team every half-finished change breaks main for everybody. Create a branch per piece of work.
  • Forgetting to pull. If you start working without pulling, you build on an old version and run into conflicts that didn't need to happen. Pull before you start.
  • Leaving conflict markers in a file. After a conflict, search the file for <<<<<<< before committing. A file with markers is not valid Python, Markdown or anything else.
  • Long-lived branches. A branch that lives for two weeks collects conflicts with everything merged in the meantime. Merge small pieces often, and bring main into your branch every day.
  • Forgetting to push a tag. git push sends commits, not tags. Push each tag by name (git push origin cp2) and check that it appears on the repository's Tags page on GitHub.
  • Rewriting shared history. Commands such as git push --force replace the history on the remote. On a branch other people use, they delete their work. Don't use them until you know exactly what they do.

Key takeaways

  • A commit is a snapshot of the project with an author, a date, a message and a parent. The chain of commits is the history, and each commit is identified by its hash.
  • Changes go from the working tree to the staging area (git add) and from there to the repository (git commit). git status shows where each change is.
  • .gitignore keeps generated files and secrets out of the repository. A secret that was committed must be revoked.
  • clone, push and pull copy commits between your repository and a remote such as GitHub. pull is fetch plus merge.
  • A branch is a movable name for a line of work. Merging combines branches; a conflict happens when both changed the same lines, and you resolve it by editing the file. A pull request proposes a merge and is where code review happens.
  • A tag is a name for one commit that doesn't move: git tag <name> creates it and git push origin <name> sends it to GitHub. It marks versions and any state that others must find exactly, such as the commit you hand in.
  • A branching strategy is a team's agreement on how to use branches. Gitflow has long-lived main and develop branches and release branches, for software released in versions. Trunk-based development keeps one branch, main, always working, with short-lived branches merged through pull requests: the right choice for a small team building a web application.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. You edited src/ledger/__init__.py and README.md, then ran git add README.md. What does git status show for each file? If you now run git commit -m "...", which changes go into the commit?

Solution

README.md appears under Changes to be committed (staged), and src/ledger/__init__.py under Changes not staged for commit. The commit records only the README change. The change to __init__.py stays in the working tree, still modified, until you git add it and commit again.

2. After a teammate's commit, git status says "Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 1 commit, and can be fast-forwarded". What does that mean, and what happens when you run git pull?

Solution

The remote main has one commit that your local main doesn't, and you have no commits of your own that the remote lacks. git pull downloads the commit and moves your main forward to it (a fast-forward). No merge commit is created and there can be no conflict.

3. Your branch changed line 3 of the README, and main changed line 10 of the same file. Do you get a conflict when you merge main into your branch? And if both changed line 3?

Solution

Different lines: no conflict. Git combines both changes on its own and creates a merge commit. Same line: conflict. Git stops, writes both versions of line 3 between <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, and waits for you to edit the file, git add it and git commit.

4. A teammate committed a file .env with the password of the team's database, then deleted it in the next commit and pushed both. Is the password safe now? What should the team do?

Solution

No. The first commit is still in the history, on GitHub and in every clone, and anyone can read the file from it (git show <hash>:.env). The team must change the password of the database at once (revoke the old one), then add .env to .gitignore so it isn't committed again. Rewriting the history to remove the file is possible, but it doesn't help with copies that already exist, so changing the password is the step that matters.

5. Your team of six builds a web application that is deployed to Azure every time main changes. A teammate proposes Gitflow, "because it's what professional teams use". What would you answer? What should the team do instead, and how does GitHub help enforce it?

Solution

Gitflow is designed for software released in versions on a schedule, with several versions in use at once, which is not this case: there is one version, deployed continuously from main. With Gitflow, every feature would be merged twice (into develop, then through a release branch into main), and develop would drift away from what is deployed. Trunk-based development fits better: main is always working and deployable, every change is a short-lived branch merged through a reviewed pull request, and branches are merged within a day or two so conflicts stay small. GitHub enforces it with a branch protection rule (or ruleset) on main that requires a pull request with an approval and passing checks, so nobody can push to main directly.

6. You finished the work for a checkpoint, ran git tag cp2, and submitted the link to the commit. Then you noticed a bug, fixed it and pushed the fix to main. Which version will be graded? What do you do so that the fix counts?

Solution

The commit of the link, the one tagged cp2: the tag doesn't move with new commits, so the fix is not in it. To include the fix, move the tag to the new commit and send it again (git tag -f cp2, then git push -f origin cp2), and submit the link to the new commit. If you had only run git tag cp2 without git push origin cp2, the tag wouldn't exist on GitHub at all: check the Tags page after pushing.

docs.title: Software design and project structure
docs.text: ledger works, but all of it is in one file: reading the CSV file, the calculations and the printing are mixed in the same functions. That is fine for 50 lines and a problem for an application that will get a database, a web API and a frontend. In this session you learn how to split a program into parts with one responsibility each, how Python organizes those parts into modules and packages, and how to represent the data with dataclasses instead of dictionaries. Then you refactor ledger into a package, proving that it still does exactly the same, and add a new command to see what the structure buys you.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. Software design and project structure. Separation of concerns and the single responsibility principle, the direction of dependencies, modules and packages, dataclasses and type hints, pure functions, refactoring and code smells, and how to design your own module.
  2. Lab: from one file to a package. You split ledger into models, storage, reports and cli on a branch, writing the calculations yourself in a starter package, check with diff that the output didn't change, add the months command, configure Ruff's rules and merge through a pull request.

"""Reading transactions from where they are stored."""

                category=row["category"],

"""The command line: reads the arguments, calls storage and reports, prints."""

import argparse
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

from ledger import reports, storage

DEFAULT_FILE = Path("data/transactions.csv")


def print_totals(totals: dict[str, Decimal]) -> None:
    for name, total in totals.items():
        print(f"{name:<10} {total:>10}")


def print_spending(spending: dict[str, Decimal]) -> None:
    table = Table(title="Spending by category")
    table.add_column("Category")
    table.add_column("EUR", justify="right")
    for category, total in spending.items():
        table.add_row(category, f"{total:,.2f}")
    Console().print(table)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="ledger", description="Balances and spending of your accounts."
    )
    parser.add_argument("command", choices=["balance", "spending"])
    parser.add_argument("file", nargs="?", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_FILE)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    transactions = storage.read_csv(args.file)
    if args.command == "balance":
        print_totals(reports.balances(transactions))
    else:
        print_spending(reports.spending_by_category(transactions))
    # TODO 4: add a command "months" that prints reports.net_by_month with

Open src/ledger/reports.py. totals_by and spending_by_category are written: read them first. totals_by adds up the amounts grouped by a key, a function that receives a transaction and returns the group it belongs to, such as lambda t: t.category. A lambda is a short function without a name: lambda t: t.category is the same as def f(t): return t.category.

Now complete the two functions marked TODO 1 and TODO 2, and delete the raise NotImplementedError line of each:

docs.title: Software design and project structure
docs.text:
What you need first

The ledger project in your repository smd-app: one file, src/ledger/__init__.py, that reads the CSV file, computes balances and spending, and prints them. Functions, dictionaries and import in Python, and Python projects with uv, especially the [project.scripts] entry of pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Why structure matters
docs.text:
ledger is about 50 lines in one file, and it works. Now imagine the next requests. "Keep the transactions in a database instead of a CSV file." "Offer the same balances through a web API, for a dashboard." "Add a report of spending per month." For each one, ask: which lines of __init__.py change?

The honest answer is "it depends, read the whole file". read_transactions reads the CSV and turns amounts into Decimal. main reads the command line, and filters out transfers to find the spending, and draws the table. The rule "spending means a negative amount that is not a transfer" lives inside the code that prints. To serve the spending through an API, you would copy that rule, and the day it changes (refunds, say), someone updates one copy and forgets the other.

In a small script that is fine. In software that a team keeps changing for years, it is the main source of bugs and slowness: every change touches code that does several things, so every change risks breaking something unrelated. Software design is the set of decisions about how to split a program into parts so that each likely change touches as few parts as possible. This page covers the decisions that matter for an application like ledger: which parts to have, how they depend on each other, how to represent the data, and how to reorganize code that already works without breaking it.

docs.title: Separation of concerns
docs.text:
Look at what ledger does and group it by reason to change. There are four groups:

  1. What the data is. A transaction has a date, an account, a description, a category and an amount. This changes only when the business changes (a transaction gets a currency, say).
  2. Where the data is stored. Today, a CSV file. Tomorrow, a database. This changes when the infrastructure changes.
  3. What we compute. Balances per account, spending per category, the definition of spending. This changes when the business questions change.
  4. How the user talks to the program. Today, a command line with a rich table. Tomorrow, a web API. This changes when the interface changes.

Definition: concern, module, separation of concerns

A concern is one area of responsibility of a program, with its own reasons to change: the data, storage, calculations, the user interface.

Separation of concerns is the design principle of putting each concern in its own part of the code, so that a change in one concern touches only that part. In Python, the natural part is the module: one .py file with the functions and classes of one concern.

For ledger, separation of concerns gives four modules:

Module Concern Knows about Doesn't know about models.py what a transaction is nothing else in the project files, databases, printing storage.py reading transactions from where they are kept models the calculations, printing reports.py the calculations: balances, spending, months models where the data came from, how it is shown cli.py the command line: arguments and output storage, reports how the calculations work

docs.title: The direction of dependencies
docs.text:
A module depends on another when it imports it. The table above implies a direction:

          cli.py
         /      \
        ▼        ▼
 storage.py   reports.py
         \      /
          ▼    ▼
        models.py

The arrows go from the outside (the parts that talk to the world: the user, the disk) towards the inside (the data and the business rules), never the other way. reports.py doesn't import storage or cli. That is the property that pays off: when the CSV file becomes a database, only storage.py changes; when the command line gets a web API next to it, the API calls the same reports functions, and the definition of spending exists once.

docs.title: The single responsibility principle
docs.text:
The same idea, applied to each piece of code, has a name.

Definition: single responsibility principle

A module should have one, and only one, reason to change. A responsibility is a reason to change: a part of the program that changes when one kind of requirement changes (the data, the storage, the business rules, the interface). The principle was formulated by Robert C. Martin, and it is the S of SOLID, five principles of object-oriented design.

It applies to functions and classes as much as to modules. The old main of ledger has four reasons to change: the command-line arguments, the rule of what counts as spending, how totals are computed, and how the table is drawn. The new is_spending has one: the rule of what counts as spending. When that rule changes (say, refunds must reduce spending), there is exactly one place to edit, and nothing else can break.

A rule of thumb to check a design: for each module or function, finish the sentence "this changes when…". If the sentence needs an "and" ("when the file format changes and when the definition of spending changes"), it mixes two responsibilities, and it should be split.

docs.title: How much structure
docs.text: Separation of concerns can be overdone. A program split into thirty files of five lines each, with layers that only pass calls through, is as hard to change as one big file, because every change now visits many places. The goal is one module per concern that really changes on its own, not as many modules as possible. Four modules for ledger is enough; a large application has the same four layers, each one a package with several modules.

docs.title: Modules and packages in Python
docs.text:
Definition: module and package

A module is a .py file. Its name, without .py, is what you import: the file reports.py is the module reports.

A package is a folder of modules with an __init__.py file. The folder src/ledger/ is the package ledger, and src/ledger/reports.py is the module ledger.reports.

Inside the package, modules import each other by their full name, starting at the package. These are absolute imports, and they work the same from any module and from any folder you run the program in:

from ledger.models import Transaction    # one name from a module
from ledger import reports, storage      # whole modules; then reports.balances(...)

__init__.py runs the first time anything from the package is imported. It can stay almost empty: a docstring that says what the package is. Before, all of ledger lived in it; now each concern has its own module.

docs.title: The src layout and the entry point
docs.text:
ledger uses the src layout: the package is in src/ledger/, not in the project's top folder. uv installs the package into .venv in editable mode (the environment points to your src folder, so your edits are used at once), and the code always runs as the installed package ledger. Without the src folder, Python could also import ledger straight from the current folder, and code that works on your laptop could fail once installed somewhere else.

The command ledger is declared in pyproject.toml:

[project.scripts]
ledger = "ledger.cli:main"

This means: the command ledger imports the module ledger.cli and calls its function main. When main moves from __init__.py to cli.py, this line must change from "ledger:main" to "ledger.cli:main". uv run notices that pyproject.toml changed and reinstalls the project before running it.

docs.title: Circular imports
docs.text: If reports.py imports cli.py and cli.py imports reports.py, Python starts loading one, has to load the other halfway through, and fails with ImportError: cannot import name ... (most likely due to a circular import). With dependencies in one direction, from the outside to the inside, this can't happen. A circular import is almost always a sign that two modules share a concern, or that a module is reaching outwards.

docs.title: Data as classes: dataclasses
docs.text:
In the one-file ledger, a transaction is a dictionary: {"date": "2026-01-01", "account": "checking", ..., "amount": Decimal("-950.00")}. Dictionaries are flexible, and that is their problem as data models. Nothing says which keys a transaction has. A typo, t["amout"], is only found when that line runs. The editor can't complete t["... for you, and the date is a string that every piece of code has to remember to parse.

A dataclass declares the shape of the data once. You write the fields and their types, and Python generates the rest: a constructor, a readable repr, and comparison with ==.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Transaction:
    date: date
    account: str
    description: str
    category: str
    amount: Decimal


rent = Transaction(date(2026, 1, 1), "checking", "Rent", "housing", Decimal("-950.00"))
print(rent)

Transaction(date=datetime.date(2026, 1, 1), account='checking', description='Rent', category='housing', amount=Decimal('-950.00'))

print(rent.amount, rent.date.month)

-950.00 1

Each field is an attribute, rent.amount, so the editor completes it and Ruff and Pylance flag a misspelled one before the code runs. The date is a real date, so rent.date.month works without parsing a string.

The annotations (amount: Decimal) are type hints. Python doesn't check them when the program runs: Transaction(..., amount="lots") is accepted. Tools do check them, and the editor uses them to tell you what each value is. They also document the code: a reader knows what balances returns from its signature, def balances(transactions: Iterable[Transaction]) -> dict[str, Decimal], without reading its body.

frozen=True makes the objects immutable: once created, their fields can't change. A transaction that happened doesn't change, and immutable objects can be passed to any function without the risk that it modifies them behind your back:

from dataclasses import FrozenInstanceError

try:
    rent.amount = Decimal("0")
except FrozenInstanceError as error:
    print("FrozenInstanceError:", error)

FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'amount'

docs.title: Pure functions at the centre
docs.text:
Look at the functions of reports.py in the lab: they receive transactions and return dictionaries. They don't open files, print, read the clock or ask the user anything.

Definition: pure function and side effect

A side effect is anything a function does besides returning a value: reading or writing a file or a database, printing, reading the clock, changing a global variable.

A pure function has no side effects, and its result depends only on its arguments: called twice with the same arguments, it returns the same result.

Pure functions are the easiest code to understand and to check. To know whether spending_by_category is right, build a few transactions by hand and look at the result. No file, no database, no terminal:

from collections import defaultdict


def totals_by(transactions, key):
    totals = defaultdict(Decimal)
    for t in transactions:
        totals[key(t)] += t.amount
    return dict(totals)


def is_spending(t):
    return t.amount < 0 and t.category != "transfer"


def spending_by_category(transactions):
    spending = [t for t in transactions if is_spending(t)]
    totals = totals_by(spending, key=lambda t: t.category)
    return {c: -total for c, total in sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])}


sample = [
    Transaction(date(2026, 1, 1), "checking", "Rent", "housing", Decimal("-950.00")),
    Transaction(date(2026, 1, 2), "checking", "Carrefour", "groceries", Decimal("-65.15")),
    Transaction(date(2026, 1, 3), "checking", "To savings", "transfer", Decimal("-300.00")),
    Transaction(date(2026, 1, 4), "checking", "Salary", "income", Decimal("2600.00")),
]
print(spending_by_category(sample))

{'housing': Decimal('950.00'), 'groceries': Decimal('65.15')}

The transfer and the salary are not spending, and the result says so. This is the shape of a design that is easy to test: side effects at the edges (storage reads, cli prints) and pure logic at the centre (reports). Program bugs are mostly in the logic, and the logic is the part you can check with four lines of data.

totals_by takes key, a function that says how to group, instead of a column name: key=lambda t: t.category. A lambda is a short function without a name; lambda t: t.category is the same as def f(t): return t.category. Passing a function makes totals_by work for any grouping, including ones that are not a field, like the month: key=lambda t: t.date.strftime("%Y-%m").

docs.title: Refactoring
docs.text:
Moving the code of ledger into four modules doesn't add a feature. The program must do exactly what it did before.

Definition: refactoring

Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing its behaviour: the same inputs give the same outputs, before and after.

Refactoring is how real code gets a good design: almost nobody gets the structure right before the program exists. The risk is breaking something while moving it, so a refactoring is done with a safety net:

  1. Record the behaviour before you start. Save the output of each command to a file. (With automated tests, the tests are the record; that is the next step for any serious project.)
  2. Work on a branch, so main keeps working while you refactor.
  3. Move code, don't rewrite it. Change the structure and the names, keep the logic. If you find a bug on the way, note it and fix it in a separate commit, after the refactoring, so that each commit does one thing.
  4. Compare the behaviour after. Run the same commands and compare the output with diff. No differences means the refactoring kept the behaviour, at least for these inputs.
  5. Review and merge with a pull request.

docs.title: Code smells
docs.text:
A code smell is a pattern in the code that is not a bug but usually makes the next change harder. Naming them helps a team agree on what to improve. These are the ones the one-file ledger had:

Smell In the old ledger The fix A function that does several things main reads arguments, filters, computes and draws one function per job: parse, compute, print Magic value the string "transfer" inside a filter a named constant, TRANSFER = "transfer", defined once Duplicated knowledge the rule "spending is negative and not a transfer" would be copied by any new interface one function, is_spending, used everywhere Primitive data a transaction is a dict of strings a Transaction dataclass with real types Vague names totals, t, data used for different things names that say what a value is (balances, spending)

Some smells can be detected automatically. A linter like Ruff does not judge the design, but it catches the patterns that often hide bugs, and a team chooses which rules to apply in pyproject.toml:

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "B", "UP", "SIM"]
Rules Name Example of what they find E, F pycodestyle, Pyflakes lines too long, undefined names, unused imports (the default) I isort imports not grouped and sorted (standard library, third party, the project) B flake8-bugbear likely bugs, such as a mutable default argument def f(items=[]) UP pyupgrade old syntax that the project's Python version can write more simply SIM flake8-simplify code that can be written more simply, such as if x: return True else: return False

Most of these problems Ruff can fix itself with uv run ruff check --fix. Read what it changed before committing, as you would read a teammate's change.

docs.title: Designing your own module
docs.text:
Your application, and your module of the group product, will go through the same steps as ledger, so it pays to design its data before writing code. Write down, in the README of your repository:

  1. The entities: the kinds of things your module records (Subscription, Invoice, Loan…). One or two is enough.
  2. Their fields, with types: name: str, monthly_price: Decimal, start: date. Money is always Decimal.
  3. The relationships: which entity belongs to which (a payment belongs to an invoice; an invoice belongs to a client).
  4. The calculations: what your module computes from the data, as pure functions (monthly_cost(subscriptions) -> Decimal, overdue(invoices, today) -> list[Invoice]).
  5. The commands: what the user asks for, as ledger balance or ledger spending do.

The four modules of ledger are a template: your models.py holds the entities, your reports.py the calculations, and the other two adapt with few changes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Moving code and changing it at the same time. If the output changes, you can't tell whether the move or the edit broke it. Move first, compare, commit; then change.
  • Forgetting to update the entry point. After moving main to cli.py, uv run ledger fails with AttributeError: module 'ledger' has no attribute 'main' until pyproject.toml says ledger.cli:main.
  • Imports from the current folder. import models (instead of from ledger import models) may work when you run a file directly from src/ledger/, and fails everywhere else.
  • Printing inside reports.py. A calculation that prints can't be reused by an API or checked without reading the terminal. Return the value; let cli.py print it.
  • One module per function. Splitting by function rather than by concern gives many tiny files that always change together.

Key takeaways

  • Design means splitting a program so that each likely change touches as few parts as possible. The single responsibility principle: each module, class or function has one reason to change. For an application: data, storage, calculations, interface.
  • In Python each concern is a module (.py file), and a folder of modules with __init__.py is a package. Import with absolute names: from ledger.models import Transaction.
  • Dependencies point inwards: the interface and storage use the models and the calculations, never the other way round. This avoids circular imports and lets you replace the CSV file or the command line without touching the calculations.
  • A dataclass declares the shape of the data with typed fields; with frozen=True, the objects can't be changed after they are created.
  • Keep side effects at the edges and pure functions at the centre: they are easy to read, reuse and check.
  • Refactoring changes the structure, not the behaviour: record the output before, move code without rewriting it, compare after, and merge through a pull request.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. For each change, say which module or modules of the new ledger (models, storage, reports, cli) must change:

  1. Transactions now come from a JSON file.
  2. Refunds, positive amounts in a spending category, must reduce that category's spending.
  3. The balance must be shown in a rich table too.
  4. Each transaction gets a currency field.
Solution
  1. storage only: a new function that reads JSON and returns the same Transaction objects.
  2. reports only: the rule for spending changes in is_spending (and spending_by_category), and every interface picks up the change.
  3. cli only: printing is its job.
  4. models (the new field), storage (read it from the file) and probably reports (adding amounts in different currencies needs a decision); cli only if the currency is shown.

A change to the data model is the one that travels furthest, which is why it is worth designing the data first.

2. A teammate adds this to reports.py. What is wrong with it from a design point of view, and how would you change it?

def print_balances(path):
    transactions = storage.read_csv(path)
    for account, total in balances(transactions).items():
        print(f"{account:<10} {total:>10}")
Solution

It mixes three concerns in the module of calculations: reading (storage), computing and printing (the interface). reports.py now depends on storage, and the function can't be reused by an API or checked without a file and a terminal. The calculation already exists (balances); reading belongs in cli.main, which calls storage.read_csv, and printing in cli.print_totals. The function should be deleted.

3. cli.py has import reports and reports.py has from cli import print_totals. What happens when you run uv run ledger balance, and why?

Solution

Two problems. First, import reports and from cli import ... are imports from the current folder, not from the package: with the src layout they fail with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'reports'; they must be from ledger import reports and from ledger.cli import print_totals. Second, with those fixed, the two modules import each other: a circular import, which fails with ImportError: cannot import name 'print_totals' from partially initialized module 'ledger.cli'. The real fix is the design: reports must not depend on cli. It returns values and cli prints them.

4. Design the data for a Subscriptions module: the user records their subscriptions (Netflix, the gym…), each with a monthly price and a start date, and can cancel one. Write the dataclass, and the signature and docstring of two pure functions: the total monthly cost of the active subscriptions, and the subscriptions that cost more than a given amount.

Solution 
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Subscription:
    name: str
    monthly_price: Decimal
    start: date
    cancelled: date | None = None   # None while it is active


def monthly_cost(subscriptions: Iterable[Subscription]) -> Decimal:
    """Total monthly price of the subscriptions that are not cancelled."""


def more_expensive_than(
    subscriptions: Iterable[Subscription], limit: Decimal
) -> list[Subscription]:
    """Active subscriptions whose monthly price is above `limit`, most expensive first."""

The price is a Decimal, not a float. Cancelling is a date, not a boolean, so the data says when it was cancelled; date | None means "a date or nothing". Neither function reads files or prints, so both can be checked with a list of three subscriptions written by hand.

docs.title: Databases and persistence
docs.text: ledger reads a CSV file every time it runs, and the only way to record a new expense is to edit that file by hand. Real applications keep their data in a database: it accepts new data from the program, checks it against rules, answers questions quickly, and keeps everything safe when something fails halfway. In this session you learn how a relational database organizes data in tables linked by keys, how to query it with SQL, how to store money in it correctly, and how a Python program uses it through an ORM, SQLAlchemy. Then you move ledger into a SQLite database and add a command to record transactions.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. Databases and persistence. Tables, primary and foreign keys, SQL (SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, INSERT), declarative SQL versus imperative Python, SQL injection, money in a database, SQLite and database servers, the ORM, and database transactions.
  2. Lab: the ledger in a database. You add a database module, link transactions to accounts with a foreign key, read the rows back as Transactions, import the CSV file into SQLite, check that the reports don't change, query the database with SQL, and add the business rules for recording new transactions. At the end you tag your repository as checkpoint 2 and submit it on Blackboard.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the session you should be able to:

  • Explain what problems a database solves compared with a file, and what persistence means.
  • Describe a table with its columns, types and primary key, and link two tables with a foreign key.
  • Write SQL queries with SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY and ORDER BY, and add rows with INSERT.
  • Explain the difference between a declarative language such as SQL and an imperative one such as Python.
  • Pass values to SQL as parameters, and explain what SQL injection is.
  • Store amounts of money in a database without floating-point errors.
  • Explain the difference between SQLite and a database server such as PostgreSQL, and when to use each.
  • Declare tables as SQLAlchemy classes, and read and write them with a session, select, add and commit.
  • Explain what a database transaction is, and why create_all doesn't change existing tables.

docs.title: 2. The database module: db.py
docs.text:
Add SQLAlchemy to the project:

uv add sqlalchemy

Create src/ledger/db.py with this code. It declares the two tables and the connection to the database:

"""The database: its tables and the connection to it."""

import datetime
from decimal import Decimal

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, Integer, String, create_engine, event
from sqlalchemy.orm import (
    DeclarativeBase,
    Mapped,
    Session,
    mapped_column,
    relationship,
)
from sqlalchemy.types import TypeDecorator

DATABASE_URL = "sqlite:///ledger.db"


class Money(TypeDecorator):
    """An amount: a Decimal in Python, a whole number of cents in the database."""

    impl = Integer
    cache_ok = True

    def process_bind_param(self, value, dialect):
        if value is None:
            return None
        cents = value * 100
        if cents != cents.to_integral_value():
            raise ValueError(f"{value} has fractions of a cent")
        return int(cents)

    def process_result_value(self, value, dialect):
        if value is None:
            return None
        return Decimal(value).scaleb(-2)


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Account(Base):
    __tablename__ = "accounts"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50), unique=True)

    rows: Mapped[list[TransactionRow]] = relationship(back_populates="account")


class TransactionRow(Base):
    """One row of the table `transactions`."""

    __tablename__ = "transactions"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    date: Mapped[datetime.date]
    description: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    category: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50))
    amount: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column(Money)

    # TODO 1: the account of each row. Add
    #         - a column account_id: an int, foreign key to accounts.id
    #           (ForeignKey("accounts.id") inside mapped_column), and
    #         - an attribute account: the Account, through a relationship whose
    #           back_populates is the name of the other side, Account.rows.


engine = create_engine(DATABASE_URL)


@event.listens_for(engine, "connect")
def enable_foreign_keys(dbapi_connection, connection_record):
    """SQLite checks foreign keys only when asked to, once per connection."""
    dbapi_connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")


def create_tables() -> None:
    """Creates the tables that don't exist yet. Existing tables are not changed."""
    Base.metadata.create_all(engine)


def get_session() -> Session:
    return Session(engine)

Read it from the top:

  • DATABASE_URL says which database to use: sqlite:///ledger.db is a SQLite file called ledger.db in the folder where you run the program. To use PostgreSQL instead, only this line would change.
  • Money is a column type for amounts. It stores each amount as a whole number of cents (-950.00 → -95000) and gives it back as a Decimal, so the rest of the program never sees the cents. SQLite has no exact decimal type, and money is never a float (see Money in a database).
  • Base is the class every table inherits from. SQLAlchemy collects the tables of its subclasses, which is how create_tables knows what to create.
  • Account is the table accounts: each account is stored once, with a unique name. account.rows is the list of its transactions, through a relationship.
  • TransactionRow is the table transactions, one row per transaction. It is not your Transaction dataclass: Transaction is what the program works with, TransactionRow is how it is stored, and storage.py converts one into the other.
  • The engine is created once and shared by the whole program. enable_foreign_keys runs on each new connection, because SQLite doesn't check foreign keys unless asked.

docs.title: 3. Storage: the database functions
docs.text:
storage.py keeps read_csv, and gets the functions that read and write the database. Add these imports at the top of src/ledger/storage.py, next to the others:

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from ledger.db import Account, TransactionRow

Change its docstring (the first line) to """Reading and writing transactions: the CSV file and the database.""", and add these functions at the end of the file:

def find_account(session: Session, name: str) -> Account | None:
    """The account with this name, or None if there is none."""
    return session.scalars(select(Account).where(Account.name == name)).first()


def get_or_create_account(session: Session, name: str) -> Account:
    account = find_account(session, name)
    if account is None:
        account = Account(name=name)
        session.add(account)
    return account


def import_csv(session: Session, path: Path) -> int:
    """Adds the transactions of a CSV file to the database. Returns how many."""
    transactions = read_csv(path)
    for t in transactions:
        session.add(
            TransactionRow(
                date=t.date,
                account=get_or_create_account(session, t.account),
                description=t.description,
                category=t.category,
                amount=t.amount,
            )
        )
    session.commit()
    return len(transactions)


def load_transactions(session: Session) -> list[Transaction]:
    """All the transactions in the database, oldest first."""
    query = select(TransactionRow).order_by(TransactionRow.date, TransactionRow.id)
    rows = session.scalars(query)
    # TODO 2: return a list with one Transaction (from models.py) per row. Each
    #         field is the attribute of the row with the same name, except the
    #         account: a Transaction has the account's name, row.account.name.
    raise NotImplementedError


def add_transaction(
    session: Session,
    account_name: str,
    amount: Decimal,
    category: str,
    description: str,
    day: date,
) -> None:
    """Records one transaction in an existing account."""
    account = find_account(session, account_name)
    # TODO 3: check two rules before saving anything, and raise a ValueError with
    #         a clear message when one fails:
    #         - the account exists: find_account returned an Account, not None;
    #         - the amount is in whole cents: it equals round(amount, 2).
    session.add(
        TransactionRow(
            date=day,
            account=account,
            description=description,
            category=category,
            amount=amount,
        )
    )
    session.commit()
  • select(Account).where(Account.name == name) builds the query SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE name = ?, with the name as a parameter. session.scalars(...) runs it and returns Account objects; .first() the first one, or None.
  • import_csv reuses read_csv, and creates each account the first time it appears. It calls commit once, at the end: the import is one database transaction, so if a row fails, nothing is saved.
  • load_transactions (TODO 2) and add_transaction (TODO 3) are yours, in the next steps.

docs.title: 4. The command line
docs.text:
The commands now need different arguments (import takes a file, add an account and an amount…), so cli.py uses subcommands, as git does. In src/ledger/cli.py, keep DEFAULT_FILE, print_totals and print_spending. Replace the imports at the top with:

import argparse
import datetime
from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation
from pathlib import Path

from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

from ledger import db, reports, storage

and replace the function main with these three functions:

def parse_amount(text: str) -> Decimal:
    """Converts an amount typed by the user, such as -12.50, into a Decimal."""
    try:
        amount = Decimal(text)
    except InvalidOperation:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"not an amount: {text!r}") from None
    if not amount.is_finite():
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"not an amount: {text!r}")
    return amount


def make_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="ledger", description="Balances and spending of your accounts."
    )
    commands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    commands.add_parser("balance", help="balance of each account")
    commands.add_parser("spending", help="spending by category")
    commands.add_parser("months", help="net change of each month")

    import_ = commands.add_parser("import", help="add the transactions of a CSV file")
    import_.add_argument("file", nargs="?", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_FILE)

    add = commands.add_parser("add", help="record one transaction")
    add.add_argument("account")
    add.add_argument("amount", type=parse_amount, help="negative for money going out")
    add.add_argument("category")
    add.add_argument("description")
    add.add_argument(
        "--date", type=datetime.date.fromisoformat, default=datetime.date.today()
    )
    return parser


def main() -> None:
    args = make_parser().parse_args()
    db.create_tables()

    with db.get_session() as session:
        if args.command == "import":
            count = storage.import_csv(session, args.file)
            print(f"Imported {count} transactions from {args.file}")
        elif args.command == "add":
            try:
                storage.add_transaction(
                    session,
                    args.account,
                    args.amount,
                    args.category,
                    args.description,
                    args.date,
                )
            except ValueError as error:
                raise SystemExit(f"ledger: {error}") from None
            print(f"Added {args.amount} to {args.account}")
        else:
            transactions = storage.load_transactions(session)
            if args.command == "balance":
                print_totals(reports.balances(transactions))
            elif args.command == "spending":
                print_spending(reports.spending_by_category(transactions))
            else:
                print_totals(reports.net_by_month(transactions))
  • add_subparsers creates one parser per command, each with its own arguments.
  • parse_amount converts the amount from text. Decimal("twelve") raises decimal.InvalidOperation, which argparse doesn't recognize; ArgumentTypeError is the error it expects, and it turns it into a one-line usage message.
  • main creates the tables if needed, opens one session for the whole command (with closes it at the end), and turns a ValueError from storage into a clean message and exit code 1, with SystemExit. import_ has a trailing underscore because import is a Python keyword.

docs.title: 5. Link transactions to accounts
docs.text:
Try to import the data:

uv run ledger import
What you should see

A long traceback that ends in:

sqlalchemy.exc.NoForeignKeysError: Could not determine join condition between parent/child tables on relationship Account.rows - there are no foreign keys linking these tables. ...

Account declares a relationship to its rows, but nothing in transactions says which account each row belongs to.

TODO 1, in db.py: in TransactionRow, add the foreign key column account_id and the relationship account, as the comment describes. Account shows the syntax of both.

Hints

  • A relationship: name: Mapped[OtherClass] = relationship(back_populates="..."), where back_populates names the attribute on the other side. Account has rows, with back_populates="account".

Imported 56 transactions from data/transactions.csv, and a new file, ledger.db, in ls: the whole database.

What you should see

TODO 2, in storage.py: complete load_transactions: return a list with one Transaction per row, as the comment describes, and delete the raise NotImplementedError line.

What you should see

The three diff commands print nothing: the database gives exactly the same results as the CSV file, to the cent. And reports.py didn't change at all: storage moved from a file to a database without the calculations knowing.

Now run the import a second time, look at the balances, and start again from a clean database:

uv run ledger balance
rm ledger.db

What you should see

After the second import, checking 6698.20 and savings 1812.00: exactly double. The database kept the first 56 transactions and added the same 56 again. A database is state: it remembers what every run did. Deleting the file and importing once gives the right balances again.

The database is a file that the program generates, like .venv, and it must not be committed:

docs.title: 7. Look inside the database
docs.text:
The database is a file in a standard format. Python includes a SQL prompt for it, python -m sqlite3. Open it, and type each query at the sqlite> prompt, ending it with ;:

uv run python -m sqlite3 ledger.db

SELECT * FROM accounts;

(1, 'checking')
(2, 'savings')

(25, '2026-02-10', 1, 'Gym membership', 'health', -3990)

Your query: write the SQL query that gives the balance of each account by name, in cents. Then leave with .quit.

The name is in accounts and the amounts are in transactions: you need a JOIN on the foreign key, a SUM and a GROUP BY (see SQL).

('checking', 334910) and ('savings', 90600): the same balances, in cents.

docs.title: 8. Record new transactions
docs.text:
This is what the CSV version couldn't do:

uv run ledger add checking -12.50 restaurants "Lunch with a client" --date 2026-03-31
uv run ledger add savings 15.00 interest "Bonus interest" --date 2026-03-31
uv run ledger balance
What you should see

Added -12.50 to checking and Added 15.00 to savings, and then the balances 3336.60 and 921.00. Run uv run ledger balance again, or open a new terminal: the transactions are still there. They are persistent: they live in ledger.db, not in the program's memory.

Now try two transactions that break the rules:

uv run ledger add credit -5 restaurants "Coffee"
uv run ledger add checking -1.005 restaurants "Coffee"
What you should see

Two tracebacks. The first ends in IntegrityError: NOT NULL constraint failed: transactions.account_id: there is no account called credit, so the transaction has no account, and the database refuses it. The second ends in ValueError: -1.005 has fractions of a cent, raised by Money. The data is safe, but the user gets a wall of text.
